articles.title: Frederick Douglass Had a Radical Respect for the Constitution
articles.author: Bradley Rebeiro
articles.content: Is the US Constitution for or against slavery? Questions concerning the legacy of America’s founding and how to interpret the Constitution have long gripped public discourse; in recent years they have become inseparable. From the 1980s came the originalists, a group of legal theorists who sought to recover the Constitution’s original meaning through textual analysis buttressed by historical investigation. Adhering to the document’s original meaning, they argue, promotes institutional stability and the rule of law. Scholars have long contested these claims, challenging the plausibility of recovering an “original meaning” or doubting the authoritative nature of such meaning even if discovered. Recently, however, a second phenomenon has brought constitutional discourse closer to political discourse. The 1619 Project has inspired new attacks against the originalist normative claim, as it recasts the nation’s history in terms of its legacy as a slaveholding nation committed to white supremacy. Scholars are now challenging originalism on the grounds that it is part and parcel of a tradition of oppression that cannot demand a people’s loyalty, much less respect. This reframes the question from the accessibility of original meaning and its authoritative nature to the problem of original meaning as it relates to constitutional evils. Still, originalists continue to defend the founding of the United States as a moment that instilled constitutional norms worth preserving. Indeed, they are compelled to do so. Originalism would not be worth its salt — promoting stability and the rule of law — if it meant only preserving oppression and white supremacy. Increasingly, we find two historical accounts representing two mutually exclusive Americas: an America founded on perpetuating slavery and white supremacy versus an America dedicated to liberty and equality. This clash of narratives is hardly new. The antebellum period was rife with political disputes concerning the future of slavery. Proslavery and antislavery advocates alike turned to the past to measure America as it was against what it should be. Slavery’s defenders argued that the institution was a positive good and that the framers of the Constitution enshrined protections for it. Fidelity to the founding of the nation, in their view, required protecting slavery as an indispensable American institution. Antislavery advocates, alternatively, argued that the Constitution did not recognize slavery as a positive good but set it on a course for eventual extinction. Defenders of slavery and antislavery advocates used conflicting interpretive frameworks to justify their respective understandings of the Constitution’s treatment of slavery. As is the case in the present day, both narratives posited conflicting accounts concerning history and its authoritative grip on the present. Still, both sides recognized that, at some level, one could not chart a course for a future that had no regard for the debt owed to the past. Frederick Douglass’s Alternative There is one figure in history who is uniquely positioned to shed light on complex nineteenth-century constitutional development and to speak to our current constitutional-political moment: Frederick Douglass, the former slave turned radical activist turned statesman. Modern-day critics and proponents of the Constitution’s beginnings alike reference the controversial conclusion in his famous speech “What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?” that the Constitution was a “GLORIOUS LIBERTY DOCUMENT.” In that speech, Douglass has many rhetorical flourishes that either side might find useful in vindicating its position on the Constitution. Those who seek to salvage the Constitution from its relationship with slavery hold Douglass up as paradigmatic of proper veneration of the Constitution. Those who seek to malign the Constitution’s beginnings tend to focus on his scathing rebuke of America — in the very same speech — as his true message. Any reference to the Constitution or the Founders in positive terms, they argue, is nothing more than a rhetorical device aimed at increasing the potency of Douglass’s censure of the nation. But both groups fail to seriously consider the method behind his conclusion. What both accounts miss is that Douglass has much more to offer concerning constitutional fidelity and constitutional interpretation than his “Fourth of July” speech. Constitutional fidelity is not to be blindly adhered to; nor is it merely a pragmatic consideration. The Constitution is truly good when correctly interpreted. Douglass’s constitutional thought uniquely answered the question of what the Constitution’s posture toward slavery was. While some abolitionists simply accepted slavery as an indelible blemish on the Constitution, Douglass sought to redeem the Constitution from the evils of slavery. Indeed, he helped constitutional abolitionists popularize a natural rights theory of interpretation that excised slavery from the Constitution. Through this interpretation, he sought to put all persons on equal footing before the law. His great task, as he described it, was “by voice and pen . . . to stand for the freedom of people of all colors, until in our land the last yoke was broken and the last bondsman was set free.” His approach to the Constitution was critical in that endeavor, and it contributed to burgeoning constitutional thought in the antebellum period. Douglass was a cardinal figure during one of the most consequential moments in US constitutional development. He was a direct participant in the antebellum debate over slavery, which set in motion several theories of constitutional interpretation. Though methods and conclusions varied, each side of the debate claimed fidelity to the Constitution through an appeal to its text and to history. These debates shaped constitutional thought during the antebellum period and carried over into public deliberation during Reconstruction. Among the throng of opinions, we find Douglass arguing that based on the text, history, and natural rights, the Constitution was resolutely antislavery. His method was based primarily on natural rights principles. He argued that the Founders built this nation on a natural rights foundation, the principles of which were pronounced in the Declaration of Independence. As such, one had to interpret the Constitution according to those natural rights principles. But studying Douglass provides more than an arresting theory of constitutional interpretation. His intellectual journey is fascinating: he discovered for himself the significance of the nation’s founding principles after having survived harrowing experiences of cruelty and oppression under the color of law. Insufficient attention is given to just how exceptional Douglass was. After he escaped to freedom, he ventured into the world of the antislavery movement. There he quickly found fellowship with William Lloyd Garrison, an experience-hardened abolitionist who famously referred to the Constitution as “a covenant with death, and an agreement with hell.” Garrison and his camp, relying on James Madison’s Notes of Debates in the Federal Convention of 1787 , argued incessantly that the Constitution was irredeemably a proslavery document and that the Union, by extension, was a curse. This left the Garrisonians only one possibility: the abolition of slavery meant disunion and abolishing the Constitution along with it. At first, Douglass adopted these views without reservation; he spoke at antislavery conventions across the North, disparaging the framers, cursing the founding, and expressing nothing but contempt for the Constitution. Douglass’s inquisitive and capacious mind could not long be satisfied with received wisdom, however. In a short time, he abandoned the Garrisonian position. As he consulted more accounts of the founding and the Constitution, Douglass became convinced that the Constitution was in fact an antislavery document, and that the truest interpretation of it would require abolishing slavery for the sake of union. Most look to him for his exceptional oratory skills, which have withstood the test of time, and rightfully so. Yet lurking under his witty remarks and fierce retorts attacking the power of the slave-owning class rested a cogent theory of law and legal interpretation. Douglass also offers a lesson for political actors who must confront the tension between their own theories and the demands of politics. Rarely does history provide an example of a figure with an intellectual stature comparable to Douglass and place that figure at the center of great constitutional change. He had a robust theory of law and justice that guided his actions during the antebellum period. It was only during Reconstruction, however, that political realities forced Douglass to act in ways that did not always reflect his theory. Douglass believed that the United States would be “complete” only when it granted equal rights to all its citizens, and especially universal suffrage. At the time, this meant expanding the circle of democratic participation to African Americans and women. But after early defeats in Reconstruction, it became clear to Douglass that there was insufficient political will to extend suffrage to both groups. Douglass’s natural rights constitutionalism had a clear answer for what the nation needed to do, but ideas alone could not bring a constitutional amendment into being. Confronted with the political exigencies of Reconstruction, Douglass pushed for African American suffrage at the expense of women’s suffrage to move the arc of justice forward. Douglass calculated the move to be an unfortunate but necessary one. As soon as the Fifteenth Amendment — which guaranteed suffrage regardless of race — was ratified, Douglass went to work again in favor of women’s suffrage. Indeed, he proves an excellent exemplar of the timeless question of prudence when confronted with this tension between theory and practice. For these reasons, Douglass remains relevant for Americans today. He teaches us much about our past and how to confront it in a sober but hopeful way. He also teaches us something of what it means to traverse adversity for the sake of justice, and how it at times might require momentary sacrifice for long-term gains. Douglass preserves the legacy of the Constitution in favor of freedom and provides a method for ensuring the Constitution delivers a brighter tomorrow. articles.title: Democrats Have Created a Consultant-Driven Echo Chamber
articles.author: Ryan Zickgraf
articles.content: “The number one rule of political fundraising,” Evan Barker writes in the first line of Nothing Left: Confessions of a Democratic Operative , “is to never, ever, under any circumstances, speak about it publicly.” Then she spends 288 pages talking about it, and it’s a wonderful thing that she does. Barker’s insider account of her time deep in the bowels of the Democratic Party often reads like The Jungle of Democratic fundraising: Upton Sinclair showed readers how the sausage got made, and Barker shows how the candidates do. By the end, it’s clear that the Democrats are a glorified fundraising organization with an electoral department attached, one that absorbs idealism, monetizes it, and then disciplines anyone who threatens its arrangements, often with the cynical deployment of identity politics. Some of the book’s most compelling sections are autobiography. At times, it’s like Hillbilly Elegy but one that wears a blue lanyard. Like J. D. Vance, Barker is a striver from the hollowed-out middle of the country. In her case, that’s Missouri, where her mother and grandmother live on Social Security checks and the towns feel, as she puts it, “stripped for parts and left behind.” At seventeen, she was cutting class to intern for Barack Obama in Kansas City, running phone banks for volunteers three times her age. For Barker, politics was a matter of life and death in the most literal sense — she has a rare genetic lung disease. Insurers could reject her because of a preexisting condition, and her parents could not simply buy their way around the problem. “My disease will kill me if I can’t get insurance after high school,” she told the law students she trained to register voters, and a version of her story later turned up in a Michelle Obama speech. Barker Joined the Dems for All the Right Reasons It’s an interesting paradox: Barker joined the Democrats because she believed they could turn a private struggle into a collective solution, but her career reveals a party that’s much better at turning that struggle into a fundraising pitch. The book follows her journey as she climbs the ladder: Brent Welder’s Bernie Sanders–backed 2018 primary campaign in Kansas’s Third District, then Adam Green’s Progressive Change Campaign Committee, and finally Left Rising, a progressive consultancy. Barker’s specialty was “call time,” the hours-a-day ritual in which fundraisers artfully beg rich people for money. Along the way, she found an unlikely professional inspiration: Alec Baldwin’s character in Glengarry Glen Ross , the motivational sadist who browbeats salesmen into following his personal mantra: “ABC — Always Be Closing.” Left Rising’s ambition was to “professionalize” the Left, equipping insurgents with the skills to navigate the corrupt political system their establishment opponents already knew. This strategy had obvious logic: candidates cannot win on righteous intentions alone. But professionalization also brought the insurgency deeper into the world it hoped to overturn. Through Barker’s career, we peer behind the curtain and watch political candidates, many handpicked by the establishment, learn the art of being a Democrat in the 2010s. This was the decade both parties got taken over. Donald Trump seized the GOP like a casino he’d leveraged to the hilt. The Democrats were captured by something softer: they tried to keep perpetuating incremental Clinton- and Obama-era politics while adopting the vocabulary of a humanities seminar/HR department. The machine’s main job was keeping the Bernie wing out. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) blacklisted any consultant who worked for a primary challenger, and Barker says she ended up on the list. EMILYs List, which she argues cares about little except money, lined up early behind the establishment candidate, Sharice Davids, against Welder. In Omaha, in 2018, the House Majority PAC pulled its money out of left-populist Kara Eastman’s winnable race in the home stretch, and she lost to the Republican. Barker is convinced that the Third Way and the establishment preferred this outcome, even if it meant handing a seat to the GOP. In Texas, she claims that the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) helped plant a spoiler candidate to drain Latino votes from Cristina Tzintzún Ramírez’s Senate primary. And in an election twist that Jacobin readers are no doubt familiar with, Elizabeth Warren smeared Bernie as a sexist on a debate stage in 2020. Barker is less successful with her half-hearted criticisms of the Bernie left (if the insurgents are too pure and the establishment is bought, where exactly is a left-winger supposed to go?) and the man himself, who has the gall to ask for his water bottles at rallies to be stripped of their labels — how dare he ! Many of Barker’s other observations and behind-the-scenes details ring as grimly funny. Her working theory is that politicians are often high-functioning psychopaths, and she teaches trainees a taxonomy of candidate types. Gavin Newsom is “The Machine.” Jasmine Crockett is “The Influencer,” convinced she’ll go viral and raise millions — no matter where those millions come from (the crypto industry, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee). Last on the list comes “The Lost Cause,” which is “regular people who are running for the right reasons but who lack the ruthlessness required to fundraise.” Her example: “No one you’ve ever heard of.” Fittingly, Barker eventually ends up at a fundraiser in Alec Baldwin’s New York home, surrounded by portraits of Civil War generals and a jelly bean tower. Baldwin, gruff in public, turns out to be warm and curious in private, asking Barker where she’s from. He may be the most likable figure in the book. How “the Race-Class Narrative” Dooms the Dems But it’s not all bad. Early in the Biden years, Barker describes a moment of hope, when the Democratic Party seemed to have learned something from the Bernie campaigns. There were stimulus checks, an expanded child tax credit that cut child poverty nearly in half, and a Build Back Better agenda that was the closest the Democrats had come to embracing material politics in a generation. Then the child tax credit lapsed, and Joe Manchin killed Build Back Better. The party’s energy went instead into what Barker calls “RCN” (the Race-Class Narrative), a framework in which every economic demand had to justify itself in racial, rather than universal, terms. She recounts one Zoom call that raised almost half a million dollars for outreach to “the LatinX community,” with Christine Pelosi — Nancy’s daughter — among the donors. She also describes a bleak working environment after 2020 in which “life became a virtue-signaling contest between me and other white operatives.” If you couldn’t sh-t-talk white men or self-flagellate about your white woman privilege in Dem World, you were playing the game wrong. After Bernie lost, Barker observes, universal health care went from the primary issue to a secondary one as “identity politics and social justice issues were a good distraction for us all.” But health care is what brought Barker into the belly of the Democratic Party beast in the first place. By the time she reaches the 2024 Democratic National Convention (DNC), when she’s surrounded by goofy chants of “joy” and “Brat Summer” while her mother and grandmother struggle with grocery bills back home, she cracks. A woman with a camera asks her to name her favorite Kamala Harris policy, and Barker’s mind goes blank. She walks out partway through the convention and, as her book’s title suggests, finds there is nothing left for her at the DNC. The problem is that somewhere along the way, Barker gets red-pilled. The podcast Red Scare becomes her secret refuge (“Finally, I had friends to laugh with at the dumb politicians I was helping elect”), and after the convention she sits for a friendly interview with Lara Trump. Then she votes for Donald Trump. She presents the vote as revenge, a middle finger to the people who burned her. But the two years since have not been kind to the politics of “F-ck you.” The Republican mega-bill Trump signed in July 2025 made the deepest cuts to Medicaid in the program’s history; the Congressional Budget Office projects the bill will leave around ten million more Americans uninsured. For someone whose political awakening began with a preexisting condition, it’s a strange way to get even. To modify a line from Glengarry Glen Ross , Barker was right that the Democrats’ leads were weak. Her mistake was taking them to Trump. articles.title: The Three True Pillars Of American Democracy
articles.content: The fragility of U.S. democracy is not an accident. Nor is it an inevitable product of our unfinished national slog toward freedom or proof of the inability of regular people to wisely govern their own affairs. It is instead the consequence of direct attacks on the architecture that makes any democratic system possible. Our supporting pillars are being chipped away, and if that is not stopped, the house will collapse. As anyone who has been forced into emergency home repairs knows, you have to do the necessary structural work before you do the other stuff. Your pretty paint job and new tile will not matter much when your house falls down. Our political system is the same. Our pursuit of affordability is nice, but it will be cold comfort if we fade into authoritarianism. Immediate mechanical fixes — counting votes fairly, preventing election interference, fighting voter suppression will always be important. But if we don’t shore up the foundation that makes our democratic society possible, we will be fighting a losing battle in the long term. Investor-centric capitalism will always and everywhere work to buy political power to subjugate the interests of the public to the interests of the corporation and its owners. This is a structural feature of our economic system, a straightforward result of the profit motive. This is why our failure to properly constrain corporate power has led directly to our democratic crisis. President Donald Trump, for all his outrages, is more symptom than cause. The real problem is the relentless nibbling away at the institutions that enable people to wield and maintain a countervailing power to capital. It’s important to tax the rich (to subtract from their economic power), and it’s important to build a stronger social safety net (to meet people’s basic needs so they have time to dedicate to political action). But there are three issues even more fundamental. They are the things that provide the intellectual and material infrastructure necessary for us to carry on as a democracy at all. All three of these things are being targeted for eradication by the political Right. The first is public education. Without it, instilling shared democratic values becomes impossible. Voucherization and privatization are constant threats. Thankfully, political support for public education is close to ubiquitous in the Democratic Party — though that support could erode if the pull of tech money ever outweighs the pull of teachers unions. The second is a free press. To a degree that much of the public does not understand, the level of local and public service journalism that existed throughout the 20 th century has already been destroyed, thanks toplatforms like Meta and Google. These tech giants figured out how to reap all of the advertising revenue of the media industry for themselves, without needing to produce any journalism. Unfortunately for the public, our democracy can’t function without journalists holding political power accountable — a fact that makes the economic collapse of the industry more worrying than typical tech-induced ​ “ creative destruction.” Public financing for journalism (particularly local news) is the only way to fill the gap. Such funding is being pushed at the state level, but there is currently no concerted effort to make it a part of the national Democratic platform. That must change. The costs to both the Democratic Party and to small-d democracy of the disappearance of professional journalism are too high to ignore. The third is labor unions. If you are reading this, you probably know that the ongoing decline in union power and density since the middle of the 20 th century has both enabled the rich to accrue vast new hoards of wealth and robbed the working class of the political power that it held a generation ago. Unions have pinned their hopes for a comeback on rewriting our awful labor laws. That would be great. But the Taft-Hartley Act was passed in 1947 , and we haven’t rolled it back yet. To organize enough new union members today, we need a lot more money to hire a lot more union organizers. One place that money can come from: the federal government. It’s not a pipe dream. Likely incoming New York Congresswoman Claire Valdez is advocating exactly that policy. Again, the Democratic Party must move this issue from its fringes into the center of its platform, or we are not really taking the underlying threat seriously. It is no coincidence that decades of successful attacks on the funding models of public education, the free press and labor unions have made it easy for the oligarchy to consolidate its own power. These are the three institutions that educate, inform and empower U.S. residents to participate in their own democratic government in a more-than-imaginary way. Republicans, the party of the rich, are quite open about their hatred of all three of these institutions. The Democrats must be even more vicious in their defense. Crucially, this must be not a rhetorical but a material defense. We need to declare that these three things are inalienable public goods, proper domains for public funding. We must create dedicated government funding streams to not just improve public schools, but also to create basic, competent local journalism in every community, and to enable every working person to have access to a union organizer who can help them exercise their right to collective bargaining. Journalism and unions won’t revive themselves — the legal and economic environments have tilted too far against them for that. Government intervention on their behalf is common sense, once you understand how far the balance of power has already swung away from these public-interest institutions and toward centibillionaires and trillion-dollar companies. Likewise, where do you think the negative effects of artificial intelligence are going to show up most vividly? In schools, in the information environment, and in the automation of work. The tech-fueled erosion of these three pillars of democracy is only getting started. As it stands, the federal government is the last great power center with enough money to prop up the other power centers that can serve as a bulwark against the continuing concentration of wealth and power in a few lotion-soft Silicon Valley hands. Democrats need to be unapologetic in fighting for, and funding, the schools and the press and the unions that allow U.S. residents to understand what is happening and to stand together against it. Many things are important, yes. But this is the most important. Let’s focus.

articles.title: Karl Marx Was for the Children
articles.author: Sam Fluss
articles.content: In the late 1870s, a visitor to Karl Marx’s North London house might have found the author of Capital on his hands and knees in the garden, with his grandson Johnny on his back shouting, “Go on! Plus vite ! Hurrah!” Marx was past sixty, and he would keep at it until he was covered in sweat. This is not the Marx most people picture. He is commonly known as a curmudgeon — a “salty” fellow with harsh words, not exactly the warm and fuzzy type. Saul Padover begins his introduction to Karl Marx on Education, Women and Children with just such a characterization: “In speech and writing, his attacks on those he deemed to be personal or ideological — or merely unintelligent — opponents were unsparing.” A familiar image comes to mind: Marx, unshaven, with thick hair in all directions, a towering figure in a three-piece suit smoking cheap cigars, ranting and raving with pride and contempt. But there is no contradiction between his tenderness with children and his polemical politics: he wrote some of his most passionate prose about what capitalism does to children. Marx found time for his own children and grandchildren. On Sundays, he would march out of his smoke-filled office to Hampstead Heath, where he would picnic and frolic with his family. There, onlookers could find him on all fours pretending to be a horse while the children joyfully rode him. As Padover writes, “Marx’s extraordinary love for children, his own and others, is the most luminous feature of his character. He was, a friend who knew him intimately said of him, ‘a child among children.’” Padover also paints a picture of Marx during his weekly outings: “When out walking on Hampstead Heath he would stop and play with children, who responded easily to the bushy-bearded kindly stranger. . . . Although a materialist with an antipathy for all religions, including Christianity, Marx used to say that what he liked most about Christ was His great love for children.” Marx’s personal attitude toward children offers an intimate reflection of his broader political commitments, especially his conviction that human beings should have the opportunity to develop their capacities free from oppressive social and economic conditions. Seeing the joy and energy of children, as well as the suffering of children under capitalism, strengthened Marx’s principles and motivated him to continue his fight to abolish class society. A significant portion of his life’s work and personal correspondence was devoted to challenging the brutal exploitation of children, lamenting his own family tragedies, and expressing ongoing anxiety about the state of his kin. Marx and his wife, Jenny, had seven children together, only three of whom survived into adulthood: Jennychen, Laura, and Eleanor. The other four died in childhood or infancy: Edgar, Henry Edward Guy, Franziska, and an unnamed infant son. He expressed a deep attachment to all of his children, and the loss of Edgar was particularly devastating for him; he never fully recovered. Marx gave each of his children a special nickname, and Edgar’s was “Musch.” He was the only son of Marx and Jenny to survive infancy, and he died at the age of eight in his father’s arms, most likely from tuberculosis. Wilhelm Liebknecht, who attended Edgar’s funeral, described the crushing grief of Marx, whom family and friends called “Mohr” (the Moor): “Marx sat in the carriage, dumb, holding his head in his hands. I stroked his forehead: ‘Mohr, you still have your wife, your girls and us — and we love you so well.’ ‘You cannot give me back my boy!’ he groaned. . . . At the graveside Marx was so excited that I stepped to his side, fearing he might jump after the coffin.” In a letter to Friedrich Engels on April 12, 1855, Marx wrote: Only now do I know what real unhappiness is. I feel broken down. Since the funeral I have been fortunate enough to have such splitting headaches that I can neither think nor hear nor see. Amid all the fearful torments I have recently had to endure, the thought of you and your friendship has always sustained me, as has the hope that there is still something sensible for us to do together in the world. Accounts of Marx as a parent paint him as an affectionate, doting, anxious figure who was deeply concerned for and protective of his family. He was adamant that his three daughters would grow up with a bourgeois education, and he exposed them to a range of literature and politics early in life: he read his children works by Homer, the Nibelungenlied, Don Quixote , and A Thousand and One Nights . Eleanor remarked that “Shakespeare was our house bible; at the age of six I knew whole scenes from Shakespeare by memory.” The girls were enrolled in music and art lessons and studied several languages. Marx and Jenny were poor during this time, and occasionally the family went hungry in order to pay the children’s school tuition. Jenny proudly remarked that “They are completely at home in English, and they know French well. In Italian they understand Dante, they also read some Spanish; only in German is there a hitch . . . ” For his part, Marx believed that all children deserved a high-quality education not only within the four walls of the schoolhouse, but also at home with their parents. In fact, in line with many progressive approaches to education today, he said, “Children should educate their parents.” Such a view of education as a comprehensive and lifelong endeavor enriched his relationship with his three girls, which was cemented by mutual respect and love. As indisputable as Marx’s love for his daughters was, it was also plagued by deep prejudice. While his worldview demanded equality and dignity for all, Marx himself harbored patriarchal and racist views in his personal life that stand in tension with his socialist politics. In his letters to the revolutionary Paul Lafargue, who was courting Laura, Marx sometimes adopts the view that his daughter could not take care of herself and needs to be guarded by others. These letters also include racist remarks, such as “When you invoke your Creole temperament, then I consider it my duty to step in between your temperament and my daughter with my healthy common sense. If you are unable to show your love for her in the form consonant with the London latitude, then it is advisable that you love her from a distance.” Other moments of sexism come through in Marx’s letters, from describing to Engels how his wife spent her weekly allowance — “Women obviously always need a guardian!” — to his description of his youngest daughter, Eleanor, who was pained by her love for Prosper-Olivier Lissagaray, whom Marx did not approve of: “Tussy [Eleanor] feels much better; her appetite grows in geometric proportion, but this is peculiar to these feminine sicknesses where the hysterical plays a role; one has to act as if one does not notice that she again lives on terrestrial nourishment. But this too will disappear as soon as there is complete recovery. . . . ” Here Marx makes light of Eleanor’s eating troubles and her health, attributing her struggles to hysteria and a supposedly feminine emotional condition. On the one hand, Marx’s politics sought the abolition of domination and exploitation; on the other hand, he espoused prejudices that stood in tension with those same emancipatory commitments. Marx’s thought and, in particular, his analysis of the family in Capital pushes beyond his own interpersonal limits. In his magnum opus, he investigates the impact of industry on the traditional family unit. With the advent of modern machinery and the factory system, older economic relations are destroyed, and society reaches the point where “the rights of the children had to be proclaimed” against their exploitation. But even more radically, Marx claims that industrialization, despite its brutal form under capitalism, creates the conditions for “a higher form of the family and of the relations between the sexes.” It breaks down the division of labor that confined women and children to fixed roles in the household. The Stolen Children of Capital While Marx fought for the best educational circumstances available to his own children, he was all too aware that thousands upon thousands of working-class children were deprived of those chances and forced to labor under harrowing conditions. Much of Marx’s writing in Capital explored the terrible exploitation of children in factories, workshops, and mines. Such abuse and terror of the young drove him to be unapologetic and adamant in his push for socialism. It was easy to see where these commitments came from. Marx documented the reality of the dangerous and horrific work throughout England in Capital . Some of the worst workshops were tiny cottages where workers gathered for lace-making, straw-plaiting, and straw-hat-making, many of them working from six in the morning until ten o’clock at night and beyond. Children as young as two-and-a-half years old worked alongside over a dozen people, with only 24.5 cubic feet per head, about the size of a large refrigerator. Long stretches of the first volume are devoted to the fate of children in conditions like these, and Marx’s writing on their exploitation and neglect is among his most devastating and moving; it was a driving force of his revolutionary rage and determination to hold the ruling class accountable for its disregard for human life. Drawing on British parliamentary investigations, factory inspectors’ reports, and medical testimony, Marx examined the exploitation of children in factories, mines, workshops, and domestic industries that were dangerously overcrowded and poorly ventilated. Children suffered chronic exhaustion, deformities, stunted growth, disease, and constant injuries, while their education and opportunities for intellectual development were sacrificed to production. For Marx, these conditions were not just a collection of abuses committed by cruel employers; they followed from the logic of capital itself: “Hence Capital is reckless of the health or length of life of the labourer, unless under compulsion from society,” he wrote. Confronted with “physical and mental degradation, premature death, [and] the torture of over-work,” capital effectively answers: “Ought these to trouble us since they increase our profits?” In 1853, Marx published “Prosperity — The Labor Question” in the New-York Daily Tribune , where he reported statistics on workers age nine to twenty-two and their weekly hours. He wrote: “Boys of nine and ten working sixty hours consecutively, with the exception of three hours’ rest! Let the masters say nothing about neglecting education now. One of the above, Ann. B., a little girl only nine years of age, fell on the floor, asleep with exhaustion, during the sixty hours; she was roused and cried, but was forced to resume work!! ” In chapter ten of Capital , “The Working Day,” Marx cites reports of boys in glassworks whose minimal periods of rest also had to include traveling, washing, dressing, and eating, leaving “none for fresh air and play, unless at the expense of the sleep necessary for young boys.” Not only did children work exceptionally long hours, but capital absorbed the precious time that should have belonged to childhood itself. In “Important British Documents” (1858), Marx returned to the reports of the British factory inspectors and the limitations of the Factory Acts, which attempted to restrain some of the worst abuses of industrial capitalism. Even under these laws, children as young as eight could legally work in tiny, dirty, and oppressive rooms for extraordinarily long periods of time, while a boy “having attained the age of 13 may, and is often, lawfully employed day and night for any number of hours, without any restriction whatever.” These laws provided minor limitations on exploitation without abolishing it, and capital continually resisted even those limitations. Marx later wrote in Capital that the shortening of children’s working hours by the state was necessary “to prevent the coining of children’s blood into capital.” The Factory Acts’ provisions for education encountered similar problems. Marx highlighted the ways in which children’s working conditions produced irregular school attendance. For example, children employed in printworks were required to “complete” a mandatory number of school days and hours over six-month periods. The result, however, was incredibly sporadic attendance, with children showing up at school for the chunks of time required by law and then disappearing for weeks at a time. The widespread inconsistency of schooling was organized once again around the needs of employers rather than the healthy development of the child. A factory inspector quoted by Marx captured the absurdity of this system in a single line: “Thus the child is as it were buffeted from school to work, and from work to school, until the tale of one hundred and fifty hours was told.” A government inspector, John Kincaid, visited two schools from which children were required to obtain attendance certificates. At the first school, the teacher, Ann Killin, could not spell her own name, unsure whether it began with a K or a C. At the second school, seventy-five children were packed shoulder to shoulder into a fifteen-by-ten-foot room. The schoolmaster was unable to identify these children, let alone tell Kincaid which of them were his students. Marx commented on these observations: “The educational clauses of the Factory Laws, while they require children to have certificates of school attendance, do not require that they shall have learned anything. . . . ” Under the Factory Acts of 1833 and 1844, younger children were bound by a “half-time system” under which they were to divide their day between factory labor and schooling. Parents of poor working-class boys and girls were eager to find ways for their children to earn full-time wages to assist the family. They were therefore anxious to pull them out of school, and off half-time wages, so they could earn more. Meanwhile, the mill owners were only concerned with getting full-time workers who had strength in their hands to perform the work. Advertisements even sought young people “not younger than what can pass for 13 years.” Employers opposed enforcing school attendance for half-time children, maintaining that it was cheaper and less of a hassle to employ one set of children rather than two sets alternating six-hour work sessions. Marx rejected the explanation of child labor as merely a result of irresponsible parenting: “It was not, however, the misuse of parental authority that created the capitalistic exploitation, whether direct or indirect, of children’s labor; but, on the contrary, it was the capitalistic mode of exploitation which, by sweeping away the economic basis of parental authority, made its exercise degenerate into a mischievous misuse of power.” Marx argued that the exploitation of children under capitalism had weakened the economic basis of parental authority and altered family relations through material necessity. As Marx explained in Capital , “Now the capitalist buys children and young persons under age. Previously, the workman sold his own labour-power, which he disposed of nominally as a free agent. Now he sells wife and child.” Machinery drastically changed who could be paid for their work, which exacerbated the transformation of the family. “In so far as machinery dispenses with muscular power,” Marx writes, “it becomes a means of employing labourers of slight muscular strength, and those whose bodily development is incomplete, but whose limbs are all the more supple.” Consequently, “The labour of women and children was, therefore, the first thing sought for by capitalists who used machinery.” The machine, which had the potential to reduce the many hardships and suffering that accompany labor, instead became a method of enrolling “every member of the workman’s family, without distinction of age or sex” under the direct dominion of capital. “Compulsory work for the capitalist usurped the place, not only of the children’s play,” Marx concluded, “but also of free labour at home within moderate limits for the support of the family.” For Marx, Mammon worship becomes Moloch worship, where unchecked capital’s pursuit of profit demands the sacrifice of children. So too does the health of the family suffer, as time at home is subordinated to capitalist greed. Work was, of course, common for the young before industrial capitalism, but Marx highlighted the printing industry as an example of how machinery particularly stunted children’s development. Under an older apprenticeship system, young workers progressively advanced from simpler tasks to more complex forms of printing and were expected to develop literacy as part of their profession. However, the introduction of printing machinery eliminated this process of education and skill development altogether. Instead, factories divided labor between skilled adult workers and young boys whose only responsibilities were repetitive tasks, such as placing paper into machines or removing finished sheets, that offered no chance to develop skills. Marx understood factory legislation as more than charitable relief for the workers and their families. The struggle over the working day revealed that “free” contracts between workers and their bosses could not protect workers from intolerable abuse and misery. When the worker goes to the market to sell their labor power, it seems as if they are doing this of their own free will, but inside the factory, that freedom is exposed as an illusion. Workers, according to Marx, had to “put their heads together, and, as a class,” compel the construction of “an all-powerful social barrier” that would protect “themselves and their families” from “slavery and death.” For Marx, a legally limited working day was the “modest Magna Charta” of the working class, one that finally established some — albeit small — limits to capital. Hardware manufacturing in Birmingham, which included very heavy and physically demanding labor, was a common area of child exploitation, with some thirty thousand children and young persons employed. This included brass foundries, button factories, enameling, galvanizing, and lacquering works. Citing the Children’s Employment Commission, Marx reported that “owing to the excessive labor of their workpeople, both adult and nonadult, certain London houses where newspapers and books are printed have got the ill-omened name of ‘slaughterhouses.’” Young women and children were engaged in what seemed like constant labor in bookbinding; children worked in exhausting circumstances in ropewalks and on night shifts in salt mines, candle manufactories, and chemical works; meanwhile, in silk weaving, children were worked to death turning the looms in place of machinery. But perhaps one of the most unsanitary and disgraceful lines of work for women and young girls was the sorting of rags. Great Britain was the hub of the global rag trade, with rags coming in from all over the world, chiefly Germany, France, Russia, Italy, Egypt, Turkey, Belgium, and Holland. The rags were used for “manure, for making bed-flocks, for shoddy, and they serve as the raw material of paper.” The rag sorters would frequently contract smallpox and other infectious diseases and then spread them to others. Another example of brutal work that was completely unsuitable for young children was tile- and brickmaking, where the newly invented machinery was used sparingly owing to the cheapness of labor. Here, children — both boys and girls — as young as four, were employed, and often worked longer hours than the adults. The summer heat contributed to the treacherous conditions: “In a certain tile field at Mosley, e.g., a young woman 24 years of age was in the habit of making 2,000 tiles a day, with the assistance of two little girls, who carried the clay for her, and stacked the tiles. These girls carried daily 10 tons up the slippery sides of the clay pits, from a depth of 30 feet, and then for a distance of 210 feet.” The harms of child labor, it was clear, extended far beyond the physical dangers of industrial work. The emergence of capitalist production had deprived children not only of their health but also of their moral, intellectual, and emotional development by forcing them to mature in overcrowded environments marked by exhaustion and neglect. By highlighting these conditions in his analysis, Marx demonstrates that capitalism’s exploitation of children permeated every aspect of their lives, reinforcing his belief that a just society must protect children’s dignity and capacity for true freedom. When all of this is stripped from young children, what is left? Marx wrote: “That excessive insobriety is prevalent from childhood upwards among the whole of this class, is only natural.” Similar exploitation and oppression befell women and child lace workers in domestic industry. The making of lace itself was done by machinery, but the finishing and mending took place outside factories, in “mistresses’ houses” kept by poor women. These women took orders from manufacturers and employed as many women, girls, and young children as could fit in their tiny rooms: sometimes ten to twenty, and at other times twenty to forty. The average age at which children started this work was six, and in many cases, it was below five. Twelve-hour shifts were the norm, with a mere hour and a half for meals, which were taken at irregular intervals and often in filthy workrooms. When business was booming, the workday could stretch to fifteen hours or more. In order to keep the lace clean, the children were compelled, even in winter, to take off their shoes. To observers, the children seemed to have become machines: “Even the very youngest children work with a strained attention and a rapidity that is astonishing, hardly ever giving their fingers rest or slowing their motion. If a question be asked them, they never raise their eyes from their work for fear of losing a single moment.” The Children’s Employment Commission stated that “their work is like slavery.” The preconditions for manufacturing did not only coincide for Marx with a new period of colonialism and New World slavery; the birth of large-scale industry also came about through a “vast, Herod-like slaughter of the innocents.” The young workers in the factories were recruited by means of a press-gang. Marx is clear that capitalism was born through “child-stealing and child-slavery for the transformation of manufacturing production into factory production and the establishment of the true relation between capital and labor-power.” Manufacturing required the ransacking of cottages and workhouses for poor children who were taken away, forced to work at night, and robbed of their rest. It was the “small and nimble fingers of little children” that were most in demand to operate the new machinery in the large factories. Parish workhouses were emptied of their children, and “many, many thousands of these little, hapless creatures were sent down into the north, being from the age of 7 to the age of 13 or 14 years old.” The new capitalist masters were for Marx “child-stealers,” and they appointed overseers whose interest was to “work the children to the utmost, because their pay was in proportion to the quantity of work that they could exact.” The consequences were cruel to the extreme. The manufacturer and reformer John Fielden recounted that “cruelties the most heart-rending were practiced upon the unoffending and friendless creatures who were thus consigned to the charge of the master-manufacturers”; the children “were harassed to the brink of death by excess of labour,” “flogged, fettered and tortured,” and “in many cases starved to the bone while flogged to their work.” Some “were driven to commit suicide.” These horrors were secluded from public view in what became “dismal solitudes of torture and of many a murder.” But the exploitation and murder of these children of the early factory system need to be studied carefully, not for antiquarian reasons, or merely sentimental ones. They should be studied because they remind us of what capital is capable of when its drive for profit goes unchallenged. As Marx shows, so long as capitalism exists, so too does the monstrous tendency to turn the blood of children into profit. All the evil creatures of Grimms’ Fairy Tales have nothing on the child-eating monsters of Capital . Children in the Realm of Freedom But aren’t we citizens of a new and enlightened age? Aren’t these childhood horrors of the nineteenth century things that belong only in Charles Dickens novels? According to 2024 figures from UNICEF and the International Labour Organization, about 138 million children are still engaged in child labor; 54 million of these children perform hazardous labor. Of course, the industries Marx described in Capital have evolved since the nineteenth century, but the persistence of child labor in agriculture, mining, manufacturing, and brick production demonstrates that Marx’s critique of the exploitation of children remains relevant. Across the world, millions of children continue to sacrifice their education, health, and future opportunities to meet the demands of economic production and a society organized around profit. If capitalism steals the future from children, how can that future be restored? All of the atrocities outlined above, coupled with Marx’s compassion for children, raise the question of what a healthier society would mean for young people. Critics of Marx argued that he wanted communism to function as a giant factory or workshop, where everyone would be leading a drone-like existence in a collective hive. But this is a caricature. Inspired by utopian socialists who preceded him, such as Robert Owen, Marx called for the all-sided development of human beings and the overcoming of the divide between physical and mental labor. And when it came to children, Marx was not entirely against the idea that they should in some capacity participate in organized labor. This was not an atypical position in the socialist movement. Indeed, in the instructions he drafted for delegates to the First International’s 1866 Geneva Congress, we find the following vision for childhood development combined with industrial education: We consider the tendency of modern industry to make children and juvenile persons of both sexes cooperate in the great work of social production as a progressive, sound, and legitimate tendency, although under capital it was distorted into an abomination. In a rational state of society every child whatever , from the age of 9 years, ought to become a productive laborer in the same way that no able-bodied adult person ought to be exempted from the general law of nature, viz.: to work in order to be able to eat, and work not only with the brain but with the hands too. Marx continued by proposing three different classes of children to fulfill this plan: both sexes from the ages of nine to twelve; those from thirteen to fifteen; and those aged sixteen and seventeen. Marx suggested that the first group’s employment in any workshop or housework be legally limited to two hours; the second class, to four hours; and the third class, to six hours. The third class should also be given a break of at least one hour for relaxation or meals. Marx acknowledged that children could benefit from beginning their education before the age of nine, but his primary concern was addressing how capitalism forced working-class families into impossible choices. As he argued before, workers are reduced to mere instruments of production, and parents are compelled to send their own children into labor. Marx thus insisted that society has a collective responsibility to protect the rights of workers of all ages and ensure that children especially are not sacrificed to the demands of capital. For Marx, defending and safeguarding children was not simply a matter of improving education or working conditions; it was a deep moral obligation, rooted in the belief that every child deserves the opportunity to develop free from exploitation. According to Marx, the methods of schools should be based on independent science and kept free from the influence of the state or the church. Protecting children, Marx argued, required “general laws, enforced by the power of the state”: “In enforcing such laws, the working class do not fortify governmental power. On the contrary, they transform that power, now used against them, into their own agency. They effect by a general act what they would vainly attempt by a multitude of isolated individual efforts.” Marx did argue in favor of free education for all children in public schools. But by public schools, he did not mean what is commonly thought of as “state schools”: Defining by a general law the expenditure of the elementary schools, the qualifications of the teaching staff, the branches of instruction, etc. and, as done in the United States, supervising the fulfillment of these legal specifications by state inspectors, is a very different thing from appointing the state as the educator of the people. Government and church should rather be equally excluded from any influence on the schools. For Marx, neither parents nor employers should be permitted to send children into the workforce unless their labor is combined with a real education. Education extends far beyond classroom instruction, and Marx included three core areas for what constitutes a meaningful education: intellectual development, physical education that promotes health and strength, and technological training that introduces children to the fundamental principles of production while providing practical experience with a variety of tools and trades. By integrating mental, physical, and practical learning, Marx envisioned an education that would cultivate well-rounded individuals rather than preparing children for a lifetime of restricted and repetitive labor. In the “Critique of the Gotha Program,” Marx wrote: A general prohibition of child labor is incompatible with the existence of large-scale industry and hence an empty, pious wish. Its realization — if it were possible — would be reactionary, since, with a strict regulation of the working time according to the different age groups and other safety measures for the protection of children, an early combination of productive labor with education is one of the most potent means for the transformation of present-day society. The above statement reflects a potentially controversial aspect of Marx’s thinking, since it is clear he rejected a blanket prohibition of child labor. However, this is not at all because he endorsed the exploitation of children but because he maintained that such a prohibition ignored the material realities of industrial society. Instead of advocating for a complete separation of children from productive activity, Marx argued that the problem lies in the capitalist organization of labor, where children are exploited for profit instead of being educated and developed. In his view, productive labor, when strictly regulated, age appropriate, and integrated with intellectual and physical education, could become a powerful means of developing versatile human beings with the ability to participate consciously in the betterment of society. At the heart of the matter lies a distinction between labor and exploitation. Marx did not altogether condemn work; instead he denounced the capitalist system that turned child labor into a source of profit while depriving children of education, health, and opportunities for development. By combining highly regulated productive labor with comprehensive education, Marx believed that children could cultivate a wide range of practical skills, intellectual growth, and physical well-being simultaneously. This reflects his broader revolutionary commitment to creating a society in which work serves human development rather than reducing human beings to instruments of capital. Today we may very well challenge his notion that children should be participating in any form of organized labor as young as nine, or balancing formal work with their schooling. Modern progressive education places heavy emphasis on unstructured time for play and outdoor exploration. But one could argue that we should keep the three foci that Marx emphasized — intellectual, physical, and technological training — all of which benefit children’s development. What counts as “technological training” will change with time and new inventions. Could it be beneficial if, between the ages of nine and seventeen, children devoted two to five hours a week to something besides schooling? Farming, taking care of household duties, gardening, engineering, or learning to code can all be part of a meaningful education. Certainly, most people would advocate for a healthy balance of learning inside school and outside of it; and in our contemporary capitalist society, where we are bombarded at every turn with screens and AI, perhaps some limited skill-based work could be a healthy choice for most children. Even though the conditions facing children today differ from those Marx encountered in the nineteenth century, the fundamental contradiction he identified remains unresolved. Exploitation is prevalent in both obvious and more obscure ways. Most modern children may no longer be confined to a factory floor in the same way as the children Marx described, but many are still shaped by systems that value profit over humanity and prepare them to participate in an unequal economic order. The persistence of these conditions reveals that the problem Marx confronted was not merely the heartless cruelty of particular employers or the excesses of nineteenth-century industry but the broader structure of a capitalist society that places accumulation and profit above human flourishing. This much has not changed. If children are to be truly liberated, Marx’s analysis suggests that the solution cannot be found simply through reforming the existing system; rather, it requires a fundamental transformation toward a socialist society organized around collective responsibility, equality, and the free development of every individual. Here, socialism is not only a political alternative but the logical extension of Marx’s critique: namely, that human beings, especially children, should never be reduced to instruments of production. What Marx called the realm of freedom is only worthy of that name if children are no longer denied their own human nature.
