articles.title: Owen Jones: Western Hubris Created Today’s Crisis
articles.author: Owen Jones
articles.content: In 2011, Owen Jones solidified his reputation as one of Britain’s sharpest political commentators when he published Chavs: The Demonization of the Working Class . In the aftermath of the longest-serving Labour government in history, Jones asked how working-class people came to be vilified not just by elites but by representatives of the parties that supposedly existed to serve their interests. He followed this book up in 2014 with The Establishment: And How They Get Away With It , a study of Britain’s powerful elite. His most recent book , The Fall of the West: How They Really Lost , looks at the dangerous and hysterical politics that emerged after the 1990s, the period that came to be known as “the end of history.” For Jones, the decline of the West that conservative commentators obsess over is not driven by immigration or the permissive culture of liberalism but by the self-inflicted harms caused by decades of neoliberalism. Jones, who joined the Labour Party at age fifteen but canceled his membership two years ago, spoke to Jacobin the day after the party’s conference. In this interview, he discusses the strength of the soft left during these early days of Andrew Burnham’s premiership, the origins of the right-wing panic about the decline of the West, and what kind of organizations socialists need to really build power. John-Baptiste Oduor You’ve just come back from the Labour Party conference. What were your impressions? Owen Jones I left the Labour Party about two and a half years ago, which has obviously been great for my mental health; it’s been quite useful to be detached from it. Last year, I went, and you could feel the stench of death everywhere during the height of late Starmerism. Now the soft-left element feels quite triumphalist. It also thinks that it’s going to see off the left challenge from the Green Party, which was posing an existential threat to the Labour Party as they saw it. But I think the most disturbing dichotomy was obviously the limited shift on Palestine in terms of the sanctions, which was only secured because of a mass movement on the streets. It obviously doesn’t go anywhere near far enough, but we shouldn’t demobilize people and make people think there’s no point campaigning and organizing. Gains can be secured through mass pressure. We need to encourage people to keep fighting and organizing. John-Baptiste Oduor One of the lessons that Burnham seems to have learned from his predecessor is that the problem with Keir Starmer was a communications issue. What you needed was sparkly, Zohran Mamdani–style video work to give the impression of listening to the concerns of people on the Left. That doesn’t necessarily have to translate into a left policy program if you can saturate the media with images of yourself looking busy. Many of the center-left media have taken Burnham at face value. Do you see him as offering Starmerism with better PR, or do you think there’s been a genuine shift? Owen Jones Starmerism pretended to be more right-wing than it was. I’m not saying he was left-wing in any shape or form, but he emphasized the most reactionary elements of his program, beginning with cutting the Winter Fuel Payment, attacking disability benefits, committing to the so-called fiscal rules [of budgetary restraint], and the authoritarianism epitomized by his government’s crackdown on Palestine Action. What Burnham is doing, I would say, is bringing to the fore the mild social democratic elements that already existed in that program and trying to stitch them together with an analysis and a vision. So, the seminationalization of the railways, the mild improvements in workers’ rights, and the increase in investment in certain areas are now being stitched together with an analysis and a vision. This didn’t exist before. Now there’s talk of ending neoliberalism without actually changing the substance. John-Baptiste Oduor The main challenge Labour has faced has come from the Greens, led by Zack Polanski. He has succeeded in mobilizing a coalition of people frustrated with austerity and Labour’s position on the genocide in Gaza. This constituency — much like the voting bloc behind the independent MPs who stood and won against Labour in 2024 — has been made up of Muslims frustrated by the Islamophobia and hawkishness of the Labour Party and progressive left-wingers. How did this coalition emerge? Owen Jones That electoral coalition is largely in urban England. We’re talking about the Greens and various independents, because there is also a separate dynamic in Wales, where Plaid Cymru is picking up disaffected support from the Left. In Scotland, there is the dynamic involving the Scottish National Party and the Scottish Greens. In English cities and some towns — Greater Manchester, Bristol, Birmingham, Sheffield, and so on — it’s Muslim voters who, I think it is always important to emphasize, have been affected by Israel’s genocide. But that disaffection predates the genocide. We saw Muslim disaffection with Labour before the genocide began. It’s due to Islamophobia, the so-called war on terror, the legacy of the Iraq War and the wars in Afghanistan and Libya. It’s about how Muslims have been othered during the war on terror. It’s also due to the fact that Muslims suffer disproportionate levels of poverty and unemployment and face discrimination. All of that has come together and politicized them. But of course, when you speak to Muslim voters, they often talk about issues such as housing and the National Health Service, which have affected them. There are about four million British Muslims. They have become part of a coalition with younger voters in urban areas, often in precarious employment and privately renting in diverse communities. Israel’s genocide is part of what has politicized people. But it’s also years of austerity and the unprecedented squeezing of wages since 2008. It’s important to say that I’m not arguing that millions of people have suddenly become politicized socialists. I wish that were true. Most people outside an activist movement would not describe themselves that way. You do, however, have a very politicized constituency of people in a way that did not exist before. There have been waves of political events. The Iraq War was the first major one. Then came the crash and austerity; the social and economic impacts of COVID-19, which are sometimes forgotten; the genocide; and Starmer’s inadequate response to the UK’s broken economic and social system. The question is, when will the contradictions of Burnhamism come to the fore? I think that is likely to happen [next month] when the budget is announced. We can see previews of what might come in Labour’s attack on the triple lock [which increases the value of state pensions each year in line with inflation]. Getting rid of it will hurt younger people in the future because younger people are aspirational pensioners. But whatever the Greens say or do now, they are going to struggle during the honeymoon period of Burnhamism. Burnhamism emerged because of pressure from the left flank, and it is trying to deal with that to restore Labour’s hegemony. There were genuine fears among sections of the Labour hierarchy that they were going to lose their hegemony over the progressive bloc permanently. Restoring that hegemony is what they are focusing on now. The underlying essentials will reassert themselves. John-Baptiste Oduor You argue in your book that many of the problems Western democracies face are the products of poor decisions they made after the 1990s “end of history” period. Owen Jones It was the economic, military, and moral triumphalism that followed the end of the Cold War that led to their downfall. In the 1990s, the West created an ever more financialized system based on extraction rather than investment, ever greater deindustrialization, and ever more complex financial products instead of making things. Companies increasingly gave money to shareholders in the form of share buybacks and dividends. Even before the crash, you saw stagnating and falling wages for huge numbers of people. Then you got military adventurism based on the same principle: “We’ve won. It’s the end of history. Our military opponents are no more, so we can do as we see fit.” It was all underpinned by moral triumphalism. Those forces collided. The wars [in Iraq and Afghanistan] cost vast sums of money, which in the case of the United States diverted huge amounts of money away from the economy and weakened it when the financial crash happened. At the same time, the reason the far right has risen in the way it has is that the dogma that “There Is No Alternative” collided with what I call a great reverse. To restore the old system, there was a full-scale attack on living standards, security, the public realm, and economic and social rights. That led people to believe they were in a zero-sum game, competing for ever-scarcer resources. At the same time, there was population movement fueled by the instability created by Western wars, and that became the scapegoat for the wreckage. People felt, or were encouraged to believe, that if there was no alternative to the economic system, their lives could only be improved by removing competition. That meant migrants and refugees, as well as various stigmatized minorities. This is what the far right has fed on, particularly in the age of the war on terror. In this context, Muslims have been racialized and cast as an existential menace. John-Baptiste Oduor The ongoing war between Russia and Ukraine is, you argue in your book, related to this Western hubris. Could you talk us through this? Owen Jones With Russia, you see economic and military triumphalism collide with each other. After the Soviet Union collapsed, shock therapy was promoted. That was the jewel in the crown of post-1991 triumphalism. Russian elites did not have a gun to their heads. Leon Trotsky noted in The Revolution Betrayed that the Soviet bureaucracy lacked property rights. It had privileges conferred by the state, and it wasn’t a class; it was a caste. With the restoration of capitalism, he predicted, it could become a class. Instead of having privileges, it would have property rights. You saw that with a receptive section of the Soviet bureaucracy becoming the new so-called oligarchy. It happened during a period of capitalist triumphalism. Neoliberalism was hegemonic in the West and was actively promoted by Western states, economists, and institutions, including the International Monetary Fund. That led to the worst peacetime economic collapse of any industrialized nation other than Ukraine, which had a slightly worse economic collapse at the same time. I interviewed Wayne Merry, who was the chief political analyst at the US embassy, for my book. He is not a left-winger in any shape or form, but he saw the political and economic consequences of shock therapy. He saw a society unraveling, a collapse in life expectancy and health, and an explosion in poverty, with people begging and starving in the streets. In 1994, he sent a memo warning that, although Russia was then a pro-Western state with pro-Western leadership, the situation would lead to antidemocratic and anti-Western elements triumphing and to a return to an adversarial relationship between the West and Russia. At the same time, in terms of NATO and the Western military bloc expanding toward Russia, George F. Kennan, the American diplomat who coined the term “containment” and was the architect of postwar containment policy toward the Soviet Union, was not a tankie. The West had promised not to expand NATO to the Soviet leadership when the Soviet Union was collapsing. The private view of the West, according to the declassified documents, was that Russia was weak but would not always remain so. It was weak because of the economic collapse and the policies the West had promoted. The view was that while Russia was weak and unable to resist, NATO should expand as far as possible. It was a kind of insurance policy and a form of containment. Kennan and other American establishment figures warned that this would provoke hostility from Russia. Even the pro-Western elite in Russia was infuriated and enraged by it. It was responding partly to sentiments within Russian society. You had a combination of economic ruin and the mass anger and disillusionment that this caused, as well as a sense of humiliation at the West. At the same time, Boris Yeltsin shelled the legislature and possibly killed hundreds of people in 1993, with the active support of the West. He helped rig the 1996 presidential election with Western support. That helped discredit democracy as a concept in Russia, because people associated what they called democracy with an oligarchic, authoritarian, and undemocratic regime. I’m not saying everything is always caused by the West. There are other factors and other social forces at play. But the West played a pivotal role in creating the conditions out of which Putinism emerged. It’s pointless pretending otherwise. It’s simply what happened. John-Baptiste Oduor At points, it seems like you treat the decline of the West as entirely a product of the choices of elites. But weren’t elites up against real structural constraints? The lack of competitiveness of European industry in a world of Chinese growth is a real thing. Declining birth rates are real — so too is the effect that they’re going to have on the tax base of Western democracies, in a world where the ratio of workers to dependents will change radically. Similarly, the fact that large parts of the constituencies of the Left are very invested in supranational and antidemocratic institutions like the United Nations and the European Union has made left politics practically incoherent. These don’t seem like issues that can be reduced to mistaken decisions. It seems like there’s a deeper problem with the left alternative. Owen Jones First of all, the West would be in decline anyway. The argument in my book is that the West’s decline was inevitable. My point about triumphalism is that it makes the decline chaotic because the West behaves as though it’s stronger than it is, given the material conditions. Its economic supremacy obviously causes problems. By doubling down on an economic system that benefits elites and is about extraction rather than investment, the West creates dire consequences. Military adventurism assumes that Western military supremacy existed in the way they thought it did. That is a case of triumphalism colliding with reality. It’s important to make the point that Western decline was always going to happen, but it has become chaotic because Western elites opportunistically used the end of history moment for their own benefit. In terms of the wider challenges for the Left, of course, it’s not simply a case of there being an economic order based on extraction rather than investment, or of the balance shifting in favor of capital over labor. There are other wider structural problems in Western societies that we must address. That’s definitely true; an aging population is one example. Even if you restore the old social democratic consensus that existed, which the Left wanted to transcend, it was based on a broader tax base. One of the clever things the [2010 Conservative–Liberal Democrat] coalition government did was to further undermine that. So, if we simply increased taxes on the top 5 percent or on big business, it’s unclear whether that would even produce the revenues we need. The book isn’t about the West in general. It’s about why the West is in chaotic decline and how that has led to the rise and resurgence of far-right authoritarianism. The Left in the 2010s began to reemerge as a political force. It didn’t exist in 2008, when the financial crash happened, as a meaningful, coherent force. It was fragmented and defined by what it was against, not what it was for. It didn’t have a coherent vision for the world of capitalist globalization, the end of the triumphalism at the end of the Cold War, or what that meant for the Left and the defeats suffered by labor movements. It started to reemerge in the mid-2010s through Corbynism, Syriza, Podemos, Bernie Sanders, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, and similar movements. But these movements didn’t have the political experience or the economic vision that already existed. They were suddenly put in very adverse political circumstances and had to learn at the same time. The Left is intellectually in a much better position than it was in terms of developing a vision to deal with the world as it actually is, with all the challenges that go beyond the basic problems of the economic system. That doesn’t mean we have resolved all our internal contradictions. The Left’s coalition includes people who are socially progressive and socially conservative. It includes people who have more illusions in existing institutions than others do. It includes people who emphasize social progress more than challenging the economic order. That’s why I think the danger for the Left, particularly in the so-called culture wars, which were a manufactured backlash against the rights and demands of minorities, is allowing itself to be caricatured as obsessed with identity politics. This is what happens when class is stripped out of the equation. Mamdani hasn’t thrown migrants or trans people under the bus. He’s focused on the economic issues that unite and transcend the divisions within the Left’s internal coalition. He obviously has people voting for and supporting him who don’t have good politics when it comes to trans people or migrants, but he hasn’t conceded anything to them. He’s focused on what unites an otherwise divided coalition. I think that’s what we have to learn from. John-Baptiste Oduor Mamdani was partly a product of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), which is a party-like organization capable of engaging in political education and cadre formation. Nothing like it exists in the UK. Attempts to create an equivalent organization that is outside of a mainstream party but able to act on it have largely failed. Do you think the Left needs something like an organization with a party-like structure to be able to wield electoral power effectively? Owen Jones I think so. The reason that an organization like this hasn’t come into existence in the UK is that the circumstances are different. In the United States, the Democrats are not really a political party in the way we have political parties in Europe. The negative side of this amorphousness is that they are traditionally dominated by corporate interests and lack democratic structures. At the same time, in Britain, if the Labour leader wants to get rid of a candidate, they can simply do it. That’s what Starmer tried to do. He carried out a purge of the Left within the Labour Party. You can’t do that in the Democratic Party. You can’t arbitrarily exclude anyone. It doesn’t matter what Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez says or does; they can’t get rid of her. What they can do, and what the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) has done, is use big money to defeat candidates. That got rid of Cori Bush, for example. But I think that strategy has hit the buffers, because the backlash against AIPAC is so great that it has diminishing returns. In the age in which we live, partly because of the internet, the Left can raise money on a mass scale. Bernie Sanders pioneered that on the Left. Through online crowdfunding, you can challenge the power of big money in politics in a way you couldn’t before. DSA can stand aside from formal party politics because it isn’t an entryist organization in the Democrats. You can operate that way because the Democrats are an amorphous party in which individual candidates are selected through highly personalized primary competitions. Those competitions rely on building a war chest of money and resources and a grassroots army to get candidates selected. You can’t do that in Britain. Instead, you have a closed selection system in which the National Executive Committee of the Labour Party draws up a long list and a shortlist and can easily prevent someone like AOC from being elected. That is why left-wing candidates have to emerge primarily through the Green Party. You have a pool of progressive people in which anyone who wants to put themselves forward can do so and they’re not in a massive internal competition to get selected for a particular seat. John-Baptiste Oduor A friend of the magazine, Anton Jäger, published a book called Hyperpolitics , and one of its arguments is about the effects that deinstitutionalization has had on the Left. In the UK, what you have is a center left that is highly institutionalized. That means outsiders can’t challenge the Labour Party, whereas in the United States the Left is incredibly weak and lacking in institutions, so outsiders are able to take over the Democratic Party, at least in primaries. Envy of Mamdani often, to me, dovetails into envy of American political fragmentation. The latter opens the door to a certain kind of chaos. Owen Jones I’ve seen clips from some DSA conferences. I feel bad because the clips I’ve seen are generally rage bait posted by right-wing accounts, but it’s difficult not to have concerns about the way political discourse works within organizations that are so open. I don’t want to pile on that person whose comments went viral, so I’ll stop here. The problem is that you need a political environment that is inclusive and allows representation, particularly of underrepresented minorities. That remains a major problem for the Left. People from privileged backgrounds often end up dominating, and we have to rectify that. At the same time, I think Yascha Mounk had a point in his book The Identity Trap , where he argued that a culture had emerged in which people defer to what is defined as lived experience. That can produce conflicting outcomes, because conflicts arise between people with different lived experiences. And these conflicts can be very difficult to resolve. A fear of discipline can emerge because discipline is seen as authoritarian or not inclusive. But you need discipline, leadership, focus, and a Left that addresses people’s actual material conditions. It needs to speak to where the working class is and address its priorities. Otherwise we are never going to achieve mass support. Mamdani is a good example of that. He’s perhaps the most disciplined person I’ve ever seen. When someone heckles him , he brings the discussion back to the cost of living: “I want to fight for the right of that heckler to be able to live in New York so he can keep heckling me.” A Left that abandons or throws minorities under the bus is not a Left I want to be part of, and it is not worthy of the name. That doesn’t mean we can’t build a Left that focuses on uniting the working class as a rainbow coalition. articles.title: The Vendetta Against Gino Has Nothing to Do With Justice
articles.author: Harrison Stetler
articles.content: Albanian-born activist Rexhino Abazaj faces imminent extradition from France to Germany, where he is wanted for charges of violent assault against neo-Nazi plaintiffs. One remaining hurdle was France’s Court of Cassation, which this Wednesday ruled in favor of a lower court’s ruling from last month that validated Berlin’s issuance of a European Arrest Warrant (EAW). Abazaj, better known as Gino among friends and allies, could now face up to ten years behind bars if he is convicted in Germany. Beneath the procedural complexities, Gino’s case represents one front in a sprawling legal tug-of-war that began in Budapest back in February 2023. Taking to the streets of the Hungarian capital, he was among the scores of activists that counterprotested that year’s Day of Honor rally, one of the largest annual gatherings for Europe’s ultraright and neo-Nazi scenes. The confrontation quickly degenerated into violent clashes, with the attendees and their antifa adversaries exchanging blows that resulted in several non-life-threatening injuries. According to the evidence cobbled together by Hungarian investigators, the injuries that Gino is purported to have caused resulted in eight days of work incapacity for the victims. For Gino’s supporters, that’s vastly disproportionate to the lengthy prison term he potentially faces should he be convicted in German court. Former Hungarian Premier Viktor Orbán’s government long sought to turn the February 2023 clashes into a morality tale on the specter of left-wing terrorism. Before losing power in this April’s election, Orbán made a pet cause of pursuing activists alleged to have participated in the counterprotests. The most recognizable public face of Orbán’s manhunt has long been Ilaria Salis, an Italian member of the European Parliament who was arrested in Hungary and elected to office during her pretrial detention. When Donald Trump moved to declare “antifa” a terrorist organization in the wake of Charlie Kirk’s murder in September 2025, Orbán rapidly followed suit. “They have come to Hungary, beaten peaceful people in the streets, beaten some half to death,” he said last September. Budapest Affair In antifascist circles in Europe, the scandal is sometimes known as the Budapest Affair, referring to over a dozen individuals whom the Hungarian government tried to chase down, with varying degrees of success, from states like France, Germany, and Italy. It has been a litmus test of EU states’ willingness to condone a blatant far-right manhunt. In France, Gino’s cause has garnered the support of major artists and intellectuals such as Nobel Prize–winning author Annie Ernaux and film director Robert Guédiguian. Up to now Gino was among the relatively lucky ones. In 2024, he was facing extradition from Finland but took flight, fearing a sham political trial should he be handed over to Hungarian authorities. The thirty-four-year-old activist, who had much of his upbringing in Italy, found refuge in France, settling in the Paris area. Though he was arrested by a squadron of anti-terrorist police officers in late 2024, he went on to win his first case before the Paris Court of Appeal in April 2025, which blocked Budapest’s extradition order on the grounds that Gino’s right to a fair trial and decent detention would not be respected. (Another extradition request from Budapest, targeting Zaid A., a young Syrian national residing in France, is still before a Paris tribunal, though it is now in limbo amid the political transition in Hungary). Gino had ample reason to oppose the handover. Ilaria Salis, a teacher in Italy before her antifascist activism catapulted her into the political spotlight, was arrested in Budapest in the immediate aftermath of the Day of Honor clashes and endured a grueling fifteen months in Hungarian jail. She was ultimately granted house arrest in Budapest in May 2024, having launched a campaign for European Parliament on a left-wing ticket while in Hungarian custody. When she won office in June 2024, her newfound parliamentary immunity led to the suspension of her trial and her release from house arrest. But even that didn’t stop Orbán. In October 2025, the EU parliament finally dealt Budapest a defeat by voting down its request to waive Salis’s immunity. The vote nonetheless highlighted the inroads made by Orbán’s lobbying: by the narrowest of margins, 306 of the parliament’s members (MEPs) voted in favor of maintaining her protection, against 305 in favor of lifting it. European Arrest Warrants Gino’s April 2025 victory seemed to grant a reprieve from politicized prosecution, but a surprise turn came when his case was revived by Germany’s issuance of its own European Arrest Warrant against the activist. And this time around, the defense’s arguments about the sanctity of legal and incarceration systems — that of Germany, not Hungary — stood on less firm ground. That distinction was confirmed when the Paris Court of Appeal decided in favor of Germany’s request, green-lighting Gino’s handover this past August 19. Still, Gino’s impending handover marks a worrying new precedent. “We have never seen in European Union criminal law a situation when another state basically steps in to remedy the fact that an EAW was not granted,” Matteo Zamboni, a Brussels-based attorney who has represented Salis and is currently advising Gino’s legal team, told Jacobin . In fact, there have long been reasons to doubt Germany’s ability to act as an honest arbiter in the Budapest Affair. Even before it made the move to revive Orbán’s pursuit of Gino, Berlin proved willing to play the Hungarian strongman’s game. In late 2024, it extradited Maja T., a German activist also implicated in the scandal, to Hungary before full rights to an appeal were exhausted. Maja T. appeared in irons before Hungarian court and ultimately received an eight-year prison sentence this February. It was far too late, but the German Federal Constitutional Court eventually issued a retroactive ruling overturning the extradition. As far as Gino is concerned, the deeper problem now is that evidence of what surpassed in February 2023 is tainted by the work of Orbán’s clientelist justice system. Here is a case that was, from the beginning, stitched together by investigators and prosecutors subordinate to Orbán’s political priorities. Evidence that now appears before a German court will likely have been drawn from that compromised source. Germany’s filings in the hearings for Gino’s extradition from France, cited in the August 19 decision that Jacobin was able to consult, try to dance around this. “The Hungarian investigative file was neither forwarded by the Hungarian authorities nor carried out by the German authorities,” reads the summary, adding that, “the exchange of information between the German and Hungarian judicial authorities took place within the framework of European investigation orders.” Gino’s imminent transfer to Germany has the Budapest Affair entering into ever murkier legal waters. “In the decision not to surrender Gino to Hungary, doubts were expressed about the Hungarian legal system as a whole. Given that, how can Germany jump on a case that was built in Hungary? What are the criteria for this? We don’t know,” said Zamboni, arguing that the case should be referred to the Court of Justice of the European Union. After Orbán’s defeat in elections this spring, many hoped that Europe might be turning a new page. The saga of Gino’s ongoing prosecution — and the willingness of justice systems elsewhere in the EU to pick up where Orbán left off — tells a different story. articles.title: Red Umbrellas: First Sex Worker Pride March Organized in Boston History
articles.author: Working Mass: The Massachusetts DSA Labor Outlet
articles.content: The marchers in front of Jacque’s, the oldest continuously operating gay bar in Boston (Andrew S) By: Andrew S BOSTON COMMON – On September 14, sex workers and allies gathered at Brewer Fountain under a canopy of red umbrellas for Boston’s historic first March for Sex Worker Pride. Led by organizers Rita Romero from Red Light Disco, Amanda Rodriguez from FemMenThem, and Jessica Van Meir from Boston Sex Workers and Allies Collective (BSWAC), the march both centered the public celebration of sex worker pride and the ongoing fight for decriminalization. Several sex workers, community organizers, and local politicians spoke to a crowd about the importance of the event before participants marched from the Common to Jacques’ Cabaret, the oldest continuously operating gay bar in the city. Speakers at the rally spoke on decriminalization, the importance of protecting bodily autonomy, and the contributions sex workers have made to the feminist and queer rights movements. The march was the first in Boston history, creating an opportunity to publicly recognize sex workers and their allies. Save Our Selves (SOS), Sex Worker Pride Boston, and Protect Trans Futures were all crucial supporters of the event. For some participants like Savannah Sly, the march marked a huge milestone: I have been a sex worker since 2003, and I am so ecstatic to see sex workers and allies visibly marching through Boston and demanding our rights be respected. I wish something like this existed when I was eighteen and was first getting started. Members of Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) and the Communist Party, USA (CPUSA) in attendance supported the same. Rat, co-chair of Southern New Hampshire CPUSA chapter, said: This is another step toward destigmatization, decriminalization, and collective liberation, and to be recognized for who we are in public. A red umbrella, decorated with both the political goals of the movement and aesthetics (Andrew S) Decriminalization vs. The Nordic Model The question of decriminalization has long been a battleground of policy for sex workers. One side favors the Nordic Model (also known as “end-demand”), where prostitution is a phenomenon manufactured from societal gender inequality, understanding buyers in the sex trade as the main culprit. Nordic Model organizations seek to illegalize commercial sex trade from the consumer side by targeting “Johns,” or customers of sex workers who are customarily presumed to be men. Nordic Model supporters believe that if the consumption of the commercial sex trade is made illegal, trafficking in the trade and the exploitation within the industry will effectively diminish. But advocates for full sex work decriminalization actively see the Nordic Model as a dangerous misstep that leads to more restriction on sex workers. Case studies of legalization have typically resulted in more restrictions of sex workers than protections, as the government requires sex workers to register within rigid regulations. The Nordic Model has likewise proven to restrict health care access in places like Canada , greatly increasing the number of health issues that sex workers there suffered as a result. Organizations such as the ACLU and Human Rights Watch have advocated for full decriminalization of sex work. Protection of sex workers’ right to bodily autonomy was a center pillar for many in attendance at Boston’s first Sex Worker Pride March. Beyond keeping them safe from wrongful discrimination or safety in their profession, autonomy plays an inevitable role in sex worker earnings, too. Zachary Flynn, a sex worker in the area, spoke on his own experience: In late-stage capitalism, autonomy is important. If you would rather judge someone for sex work than pay them a livable wage, then what else do you expect us to do? I work three to four jobs on top of sex work, and that is barely keeping me afloat. Zachary continued, speaking on how sex work builds wealth through labor: I think the fact that even with sex work being one of three to four jobs someone can have and even then not being able to support themselves financially says a lot on its own, but not everyone’s story with sex work is strictly about survival. It’s a chosen (and needed) profession for a fair amount of society. The point of the march is autonomy. All forms of work are selling your mind or body through means of labor, so why is it different in this context? If you have ever watched or rented porn, visited a strip club or advocated for women/queer rights, that means you support sex work, whether you realize it or not. Protect Trans Futures’ contingent marching along the Boston Common (Andrew S) From Origins to Pride Carol Leigh was the first to coin the term “sex work” in the 1980s to provide a term that described work different from prositution. According to Mary Carol of the Boston Sex Workers and Allies Collective (BSWAC), an important part of that was the emphasis on work and labor. BSWAC organized around the community around this foundational concept in the run-up to the Pride March. On September 7, BSWAC hosted a screening and panel on Working Girls (1986), independent filmmaker Lizzie Borden’s movie about a day in the life of a woman working in a brothel in New York City. An overbearing manager forces her to stay beyond her hours, while displaying glimpses of interaction between workers and clients throughout the entire day. Working Girls is a representation of sex workers and their connection to labor in the view of Mary Carol. The Pride March also took the time to remember what sex workers have contributed to and suffered historically. The red umbrellas ubiquitous across the march were not coincidence, but rather the universal symbol of solidarity that has called attention to poor working conditions faced by sex workers since 2001. Further, sex workers’ contributions far outdate the symbol. Sly stated: Sex workers helped start Pride. Sex workers are in the canaries in the coal mine for how people are treated. They are at the forefront at the advancement of human rights and bringing home the bacon for their communities at the same time. Pride is sex workers claiming their own unique space and being the focus for collective liberation. Many steps remain to make in order for sex worker pride to be fully enjoyed. Rat claimed that more needs to be done legislatively and culturally: “we need to challenge elected officials on their decriminalization stance, and we need people to speak up for sex workers even when they’re not in the room.” BSWAC’s Legislative Priorities include legislation for full decriminalization, safe reporting, and mechanisms to protect workers from sexual assault by cops. Andrew S is a member of Boston DSA and associate editor of Working Mass. The post Red Umbrellas: First Sex Worker Pride March Organized in Boston History appeared first on Working Mass .

articles.title: Brazil’s Presidential Election Is Going Down to the Wire
articles.author: Olavo Passos de Souza
articles.content: As the Brazilian presidential election on October 4 draws closer, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is in a very tight contest with Flávio Bolsonaro, the son and heir of the Bolsonaro political dynasty. Lula is leading most of the polls for the first round, but the race appears too close to call in the event of a runoff between them. This election does not merely pit two opposing candidates against each other. It is a struggle between Brazil’s democratic forces and the return to power of a reactionary bloc. Lula’s Challenge Lula is seeking a fourth term as president at the age of eighty-one. The Brazilian constitution allows for this: it does not impose any limits on how long one person can be in office, so long as they do not serve more than two consecutive terms. After his first victory in 2002, Lula went on to complete two highly successful terms. His government lifted millions out of poverty with social programs like Bolsa Familia , greatly expanded Brazil’s education and health care systems, and achieved some notable diplomatic victories at the United Nations. When he left office in 2010 with an 87 percent approval rating, most people assumed that this would mark the departure of the man Barack Obama described as the most popular politician on earth from the political scene. However, the failure of his successor Dilma Rousseff to deal with a hostile Congress, endemic corruption, and Brazil’s economic slowdown led to her impeachment — which many refer to as a soft coup — in 2016. Lula was prepared to run again in the 2018 presidential election, but the Lavo Jato (“car wash”) corruption inquiry resulted in his arrest on charges of corruption. With Lula barred from running, the far-right candidate Jair Bolsonaro defeated his Workers’ Party (PT) ally Fernando Haddad and became president. The magistrate Sergio Moro, the main figure behind Lavo Jato, soon accepted a position in Bolsonaro’s government. When further revelations discredited the investigation against Lula and revealed its chief enforcer Moro to be profoundly biased, the Supreme Court annulled his sentence and he was released. He went on to win the 2022 election after four disastrous years of Bolsonaro’s presidency before fending off a coup attempt by his vanquished opponent. Bolsonaro is now in jail because of his role in the failed coup and prohibited from seeking political office. Four years after his triumphal (some would say messianic) return to the front of the political stage, Lula’s government only has lukewarm achievements to its credit — in large part due to a hostile Congress — and it has failed to adapt to the age of social media. Lula is a figure rooted in a now bygone age of struggle for democracy during the 1970s and ’80s who reached his pinnacle in the civil and democratic 2000s. His greatest appeal at present derives from his status as the sole defender of democracy in an extremely polarized 2020s Brazil that is rife with disinformation. Bolsonaro 2.0 This amounts to a tepid appeal that is not enough for many younger voters — opposition to the far right can only carry a politician so far. Flávio Bolsonaro, who is more civilized in style but no less vile in substance than his father, has the evangelical right firmly behind him. He also has the backing of many figures within Brazil’s financial system, not to mention open support from the United States. His brother Eduardo, who is based in Florida, is almost single-handedly responsible for urging Donald Trump to impose tariffs on Brazil. Bolsonaro has suffered from a series of scandals that resulted in the viability of his candidacy being called into question just a few months ago. He was implicated in a major financial scandal with a bizarre twist, having asked a corrupt banker to finance a biographical film about his father (starring Jim Caviezel of The Passion of the Christ as Jair), Bolsonaro also fell out with his stepmother Michelle, who is herself a powerful figure among evangelicals. None of this has deterred him from carrying on, and he has bounced back in the polls with a vengeance over the course of September. This in no small part due to the fact that Alexandre de Moraes, one of Brazil’s chief jurists and a hate figure for the Bolsonarist right, has been embroiled in a corruption scandal of his own. This supplied ammunition to the Bolsonarist camp. In the event of a runoff election between Flávio and Lula, the former will be expecting to win over most of those who voted for the other candidates in the first round. All of those candidates are right-wingers of one kind or another, and the Bolsonaro camp appeals to their base far more than Lula does. In fact, they neatly represent the spectrum of the Brazilian right, with each laying claim to their own niche. The Miscellaneous Right Romeu Zema, governor of Minas Gerais, is the candidate (and only noteworthy member) of NOVO, the New Party. This is a libertarian, faux-technocratic party that promises to cut back on government excesses and do away with the corrupt state machinery. In practice, this would mean privatizing all social services and dismantling state institutions before selling them to the highest bidder. The traditional neoliberal political forces in Brazil have collapsed in the face of the Bolsonarist far right, so Zema is now the closest thing the country has to that old style of politics. His disastrous tenure in Minas Gerais, where the state debt skyrocketed during his time as governor, tells us all we need to know about his approach to managing a government. Ronaldo Caiado, governor of Goiás, is a representative of the traditional Brazilian Centrão, the “Big Center” — that is, the large, nonideological, profit-based section of Congress composed of figures who care only about preserving their own power, regardless of political positioning or policy. As governor of Goiás in the midwest, Caiado is extensively connected to Brazil’s agribusiness bloc. This bloc comprises a handful of large landowners whose properties often dwarf small countries in acreage, and who are determined to go on clearing rainforest so they can claim new land. The agribusiness bloc is one of Brazil’s most powerful lobbies, and it is squarely opposed to Lula’s environmental protection policies. Renan Santos is the political chief of the Free Brazil Movement, a reactionary, Tea Party–style movement that emerged in the early 2010s. It preaches libertarianism, demonizes anything left wing, and argues for “free speech at all costs.” The movement is heavily composed of dissatisfied young Brazilians, many of whom belong to online subcultures such as the “manosphere.” They are hostile not only to the current Brazilian state but also to many of its democratic institutions. Santos comes out with fiery rhetoric: at a debate held in August, which neither Lula nor Flavio attended, he cursed and insulted both of the leading candidates. His crypto-fascistic stances, his speeches, and his personality bring back memories of Jair Bolsonaro. However, whereas the former was a reactionary harking back to the 1960s dictatorship, Santos looked forward to a more social-media-savvy, anti-democratic future under the specter of anti-statist tech magnates such as Elon Musk and Peter Thiel. Capitalist Minds The most curious figure among the lesser candidates is the best-selling author Augusto Cury, whose self-help book and highly questionable positions on psychology have made him a rich man. Cury presents himself as a centrist candidate with a “capitalist mind and a social heart,” and is at best unclear about any major policy or position. Cury managed to reach third place in the polls, albeit with a meager 11 percent, for a few days in early September, in the midst of Flávio Bolsonaro’s many scandals, before falling back to 6 percent. Not as radioactive to left-wing and middle-ground voters as the other candidates but firmly separate from Lula and the traditional Left, Cury is the quintessential “independent” candidate. None of these candidates poll much higher than 5 percent, and all of them draw support from segments of conservative Brazilians who are frightened of Bolsonaro but will take any alternative to Lula. Lula is unquestionably a political and electoral titan, but he has not produced a successor or replacement who could give the sense that there is a younger generation coming forward in Brazilian politics. Dilma Rousseff now serves as president of the World Development Bank, while Fernando Haddad has been tainted by multiple defeats. Flávio Dino, the former governor of Maranhão, was a popular and charismatic figure, but Lula nominated him to serve on the Brazilian Supreme Court in 2024, which removed him from the political scene. Instead of grooming a replacement for 2026, Lula chose to run for a fourth term, which pits him against a much younger option. The results of the upcoming election will reveal whether this proves to be a bridge too far in his long career. articles.title: Amazon Is Perfecting Total Surveillance of Its Workforce
articles.author: C. R. Calabria
articles.content: Although Amazon is increasingly synonymous with worker surveillance , the logistics behemoth has never been a pioneer in that space. UPS was the first fleet to install GPS in their vehicles back in 1991. Netradyne, the company that makes the AI-powered product Driver.i installed in most vehicles in Amazon’s fleet, had already logged over a hundred million minutes of driving time before Amazon signed the firm on. But with each new iteration of its delivery-aid-cum-surveillance tech, Amazon has proven its knack for taking an existing product and deploying it in a dystopian direction. And other companies tend to follow its lead. “Smart delivery glasses,” Amazon’s latest gadgets, which come with a specialized vest with a built-in battery-pack, were introduced on their in-house news site last October to little fanfare ; only a couple of niche tech websites covered it. According to a recent post on r/AmazonDSPDrivers, a Reddit community for Amazon’s scattered global network of Delivery Service Partner (DSP) drivers, training with the smart glasses at some DSPs has begun. It’s not unlikely that a nationwide rollout may come as soon as this year’s holiday season. On the surface, the aim of smart delivery glasses is to replace the use of the smartphone on the job, allowing the driver to pay attention to their surroundings instead of looking at their phone. For DSP drivers, the smartphone is everything: It identifies packages, provides a walking path from the vehicle to the delivery location, instructs drivers on where and how to deliver items, photographs packages at the designated drop-off location, and requires a swipe to confirm completion of a delivery. With smart delivery glasses, Amazon promises to make delivering “safer and more seamless,” which is very likely true — I imagine, as a former DSP driver myself, that at least they will make it less annoying to sort through an overpacked cargo area. But the smart glasses reflect a larger philosophical position, one ubiquitous in Big Tech and fueled by the artificial intelligence gold rush: that the human is not enough, and that we need to be aided — and disciplined — by AI. A Formidable Surveillance Arsenal Each device in Amazon’s surveillance arsenal serves a unique function. The Amazon app tracks a driver’s location and pace in real time, sending that information to Amazon and the driver’s DSP. Then comes Driver.i. With one camera pointed at the road, one camera at the driver, and two side-view cameras, the platform records drivers at all times, analyzing 100 percent of driving time. When an infraction occurs — whether an actual infraction or one that Driver.i has made up — the Driver.i robot scolds you in real time, sending video of your alleged infraction to Amazon, to you, and to your DSP. Right now, the surveillance stops there. But with the introduction of smart delivery glasses, surveillance never has to end. Put your delivery vehicle in park, and the glasses automatically turn on. Like Alejandro Jodorowsky’s sketches of his never-created Dune , the latest technology is Amazon’s mad vision come to life: the ouroboros of watching people at work. Amazon’s model is more than surveillance. At the core of its vision, Amazon is doing what it has always done best: both spearheading and reflecting the worst antihuman impulses of our age. Its proliferation is the result of what David Moscrop calls our “ shared pastureland ” breaking. Ring cameras, for one, have been a subsidiary of Amazon since 2018; the desire to protect one’s packages from would-be thieves prompts many people to purchase Ring cameras. Last year, Ring announced a partnership with Flock Safety, the increasingly maligned surveillance company, which was canceled this February after a public backlash over a Super Bowl ad. (Flock has an entire page dedicated to how it serves Amazon.) Isolation is central to both the consumer and employee experiences. Amazon, which does not directly hire any of the hundreds of thousands of workers who deliver its packages, nevertheless pays millions of dollars yearly to union-busting consulting firms to ensure workers’ isolation, claiming that its tactics are protected by the First Amendment. Just last year, Amazon fired 150 workers who had organized with a Queens-based DSP. The year before, eighty-four workers at a DSP in Palmdale, California, successfully negotiated a union contract with its DSP; the DSP’s contract with Amazon was quickly terminated. And when workers in Quebec unionized a warehouse, the company responded by shutting down its operations across the whole province. Not only does Amazon use technology to push humans to the limits of their productive capacity at work, but it also creates tandem machine-human systems that encourage humans to become nonthinking bodies: isolated and automated. Every critical decision, from deciding how many workers will deliver in a given day (a common DSP practice is to schedule more workers than it needs, waiting for the algorithm to decide how many it can put into vehicles), to configuring routes, to punishing driving infractions, is configured by an automated AI system. For example: If the AI decides you’ve run a red light, and you can’t prove you didn’t, it’s an immediate termination. A Human Future for Work? Amazon’s plan to surveil and automate work at every step is a vision mid-implementation. The logical end point of this AI-driven efficiency is pure automation: in other words, brainlessness. The last stop of ultimate efficiency is what some people might call animal, and others might call lobotomized. Both terms gesture toward the same thing: at best, that human workers are too slow, and at worst, that human workers are not to be trusted. The source of this tendency is, of course, the long-standing capitalist goal of asserting ever-greater control over workers and replacing them entirely where possible. UPS workers, who are unionized, have demonstrated an alternate vision for the future of work. When UPS decided to install its own Lytx DriveCam monitoring system in 2022 (followed shortly thereafter by FedEx and Walmart), the Teamsters union disputed the use of the technology, claiming that it infringed on workers’ rights. What workers and the company eventually settled on was to record only when a driving infraction was detected, such as a vehicle swerving or impact, to protect the driver as much as to surveil them. To evaluate the difference between each technology, you might ask: When a new AI-first technology is implemented, does the technology actually aim to make drivers safer — giving them more protection in the event of an accident? Or is its point to punish drivers by using negative reinforcement to curb bad driving habits? You might then look at how the implementation of the technology aligns with the company’s long-term vision. For instance: Is the point of technology like Driver.i — whose creator Netradyne began with self-driving aspirations — to make the driver safe, or to ultimately make the driver obsolete? Despite our moral qualms with these labor practices, Americans can’t seem to get over using Amazon. When I worked for a DSP last summer because I was desperate (and it was one of the better-paying jobs in the area), I felt a little like my Amazon job was penance for all of the Amazon shopping that I had done over the years: for all of the delivery drivers who had come to my various houses and apartments in the extreme heat and cold; who hadn’t had a break in ten hours; who had nowhere to pee. Yet there’s no fundamental reason why efficient package delivery needs to involve dehumanizing surveillance, AI discipline, and otherwise degrading labor conditions. The unionized UPS drivers who have successfully fought back against surveillance, and the growing efforts to organize Amazon itself, point to the possibility of a more human future for work, one where collective action limits management’s ability to spy on and control its workforce. articles.title: Cape Town’s ‘Apartheid wall’ met with protest
articles.author: Nicholas Mwangi
articles.content: A proposed R114 million wall along Cape Town’s N2 has sparked protests, with residents and civil society groups accusing the city of investing in a barrier that could deepen the divide between poorer communities and surrounding suburbs. Residents marched on September 25 to oppose the N2 Edge project, a planned 9-kilometer wall development that the city says is aimed at improving safety and security along the highway. But protesters say that the wall risks reproducing the spatial divisions created under apartheid, saying public money should instead be spent on housing, public services and opportunities for communities that have been pushed to the margins. Movement for CARE, which was among those involved in organizing the protests, had criticized the project, saying; “Instead of investing in dignified housing, safe neighborhoods, quality public services, and opportunities for communities that have been pushed to the margins for generations, the city wants to invest millions in a barrier that deepens exclusion and reinforces the geography of apartheid.” The organization said from the beginning when the news about the proposal was announced, that Cape Town does not need more walls but rather affordable housing close to work and economic opportunities, as well as greater investment in communities. “We need investment in communities, not their isolation. We need a city that brings people together instead of driving them further apart,” it said. The Movement for CARE described the proposed structure as an “Apartheid Wall,” arguing that the first step towards justice is refusing to normalize and hide existing inequalities. City defends the R114 million project The City of Cape Town has defended the project as a safety intervention. In January, Cape Town Mayor Geordin Hill-Lewis said the city’s adjustment budget had committed “R114m to the N2 Edge project.” The investment “will make a positive difference to the safety of every motorist along that stretch, and reduce pedestrian fatalities,” Hill-Lewis said. He said the project would repair safety barriers and introduce other safety improvements for communities along the N2. Hill-Lewis also said that a small number of “criminal elements” were affecting the safety of hundreds of thousands of daily N2 users. According to the mayor, the N2 Edge project would be accompanied by increased highway patrols, with more than 40 new Metro police officers deployed to the N2, supported by CCTV cameras, automatic number plate recognition and digital coordination for rapid response. Despite the widespread backlash, the city maintains it will continue with the project. Abahlali baseMjondolo backs the protest Abahlali baseMjondolo also supported the protests, saying in a post that the project would deepen racial and economic divisions in the city. “The City of Cape Town continues to entrench neo-apartheid laws in post-apartheid South Africa by building a wall that segregates and hides the poor from the rich along the N2,” the organization said. Adding that the project shows that the Democratic Alliance-led City does not recognize the needs of poor communities, particularly Black communities. Read more: “A declaration of war against the poor”: AbM leads resistance against South Africa’s anti-occupation bill The organization said it supported the struggles of residents in Khayelitsha, Langa, Dunoon, Gugulethu and Mitchells Plain who continue to face what it described as segregation and racism. The protests have raised questions over whether the R114 million allocated to the N2 Edge project represents the right priority for Cape Town. With the protesters arguing that public resources should instead be directed towards reducing inequality, improving services and providing better housing and opportunities for communities living along the N2, instead of separating communities and concealing poverty.

articles.title: “The Power of Law”: Wolfgang Kaleck on Reconciling Legality and International Justice
articles.content: This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form. AMY GOODMAN : This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report . I’m Amy Goodman in Berlin, Germany, with Anjali Kamat in New York. ANJALI KAMAT : As the United States escalates its attack on the International Criminal Court, we continue our discussion with the German human rights attorney Wolfgang Kaleck, the founder of the European Center for Constitutional and Human Rights. Wolfgang Kaleck’s new book is titled The Power of Law: Reconciling Legality and International Justice . Wolfgang, why did you choose to write this book at this moment? WOLFGANG KALECK : Because, of course, the attacks against international law are well known. And what really shocked me was how little the support for international law was, and that, of course, we have, you know, the realpoliticians, in the line of Henry Kissingers and others, we have the far right, represented internationally by President Donald Trump and Javier Milei from Argentina, but, unfortunately, many liberal, democratic and even leftist people did play down the role international law played in the last couple of years and can play. And so, that was my starting point, to bring another perspective into the public discourse, in particular in Germany, because Germany — you know, despite all the critiques that Germany, the German government and German politicians deserve, they played an important role in the establishment of rules and institutions in international law. ANJALI KAMAT : Germany is one of the biggest funders of the International Criminal Court. Do you believe Benjamin Netanyahu would be arrested if he came to Berlin? WOLFGANG KALECK : He wouldn’t come to Berlin, because he knows that — he knows it. And so, it’s a fake discussion. It’s a stupid discussion. And I think even Chancellor Merz, whom you quoted when he was saying — before he was chancellor, he was saying that Benjamin Netanyahu would be allowed to visit Germany without being arrested. He, Chancellor Merz, rode back, because it’s very clear it would be unlawful. And this is also the — but this is one of the problems of German foreign politics right now. It’s not principled enough, because if you defend an institution, you have to defend the institution when it’s attacked. And I’m happy to have heard that our foreign minister went to The Hague. The minister of justice was there before. They are defending the court, and the court needs defense. You have to say one thing, you know, about the chilling effect of sanctions and everything. The court became very, very active and is very courageous since they learned about the first sanctions against judges and prosecutors. It’s not that they shied back. And that is something I would really — that is also something encouraging. You know, when you go to The Hague these days, the people are working more than ever and are struggling more than ever to fight impunity wherever it is necessary. ANJALI KAMAT : Now, one of the things you do in this book is you give us the longer view of the attacks on international law. This isn’t something that is new with the Trump administration. So, tell us a little bit about that history. And, you know, we’re also — you know, this is the 25th year since the 9/11 attacks here in New York. What role did the September 11th attacks play in the weakening of international norms? WOLFGANG KALECK : It’s about narratives. And so, one narrative is that the post-Second World War liberal world order was actually, you know, fair and just for all people in the world. And this was definitely not the case. The world was in disorder for many people in many parts of the world for many decades. And this is why I remind us from all the crimes, only the Western crimes. I could have mentioned the crimes of the Soviet Union and others, but I’m focusing on the West, not because they’re worse or better, because we live in a Western country. And one thing is, what I’m — what I’m really writing against and what I’m speaking against is this notion of, you know, there were better times. No, the times were not better. I mean, you live in a country where, you know, the Vietnam War was fought, and it went impune. You know, they bombed the country. They committed war crimes, crimes against humanity, and then Latin America, Central America, and it went all impune. But I think a main difference between back then and now is that many people lost the hope, and many people feel powerlessness also in the light of the many crises we’re experiencing right now. And this is why I want to write. You know, I want to write an assessment which is, you know, as ambivalent and as contradictory as our life and the political situation is. Yes, there were strokes, there were violations of international law in history, and there are strokes and violations of international law now. But there were always people who fought against it, and we gained some achievements, and that should not be forgotten. AMY GOODMAN : So, if you could talk, Wolfgang Kaleck, about what gives you the most hope at this point? I mean, we have never seen such a frontal assault on the International Criminal Court. I mean, President Trump, the Secretary of State Marco Rubio clearly trying to completely dismantle it. But you also talk about protests and actions that followed the U.S. response to 9/11, from the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq to Guantánamo, to the prison in Iraq, Abu Ghraib. So, talk about what is happening. And do you feel they could succeed, President Trump, in dismantling it and pressuring countries to do that, and what the resistance, the most effective forms of resistance over the years? WOLFGANG KALECK : Yeah, you mention 9/11, 2001, in this country. And, I mean, I want to remind us that the Bush administration, which seems now to be a well-respected government in the global opinion, which I find incredibly wrong, because they installed a worldwide torture system, and they started the completely blatant Iraq War in 2003, which led to 1 million lives and to much more instability and insecurity in the whole region. So, the interesting thing is that law made a difference by that time. When the Center for Constitutional Rights — and they were really the avant-garde, the icebreakers of that time — when they started their Guantánamo litigation, they were attacked. They received hatred mails. And a couple of years later, you know, in the early 2000s, they were joined by pro bono law firms in this country. They were joined by many other NGOs. And that’s an expression of hope and resistance, because lawyers in this country, including lawyers from the administration, realized that this is a frontal attack against the rule of law, and they acknowledged the importance of rule of law. And so, the idea of making Guantánamo a model, you know, to exterritorialize torture in order to close completely access to justice, that model failed. And that is due to the resistance in this country, but also outside this country. And this is, for me — of course, it’s insane that Guantánamo is still open, and most of the people who tortured there and elsewhere went impune. But still, it was an important step forward. It could have been worse. And it was also an expression of the hope that the law can be applied against the powerful in the world. And so, that’s how I read the story. I completely understand people who read it in another way. And then, of course, you mentioned the protests. There were millions of people all over the world protesting against the Iraq War. And I’m deeply missing that right now. I’m deeply missing that right now. Things have even become more difficult. We know that. But, you know, only to mention these two situations: the Ukraine and Gaza. We have the Ukrainian civil society documenting the Russian war crimes from day one, with all the costs. And even under very much worse conditions, the Palestinian organizations, journalists, photographers, human rights lawyers are documenting Israeli crimes in Gaza — and, of course, please don’t forget the West Bank. They are documenting these crimes in order to bring cases, in order — and that is inspired by the hope that someday there will be something like justice. And I call my own people in Germany, but also here in New York. I mean, it’s irresponsible to leave them alone. You know, if they do this work under these conditions, we have the obligation, you know, to stay in solidarity, rather than lamenting, drinking wine and going on to our country houses and play music and yoga. ANJALI KAMAT : Wolfgang, you invoke Gramsci’s famous edict: “pessimism of the intellect, optimism of the will.” You know, how has that guided this book and your life’s work? WOLFGANG KALECK : I mean, we have to be very clear in the assessment of the current political situation. It’s not good. It’s not good at all. But remember, Antonio Gramsci, the Italian communist, wrote this famous quote and all his thoughts in a fascist prison, you know? And this guy, you know, guided us all over the years, because he and many other thinkers of that time were very clear. The time will come when, you know, we have again the possibility to establish a free and just society. And that is also something, you know. With all humility, we have to understand that others were struggling for the same goals a while ago — the workers’ movement, the feminist movement, the U.S. civil rights movement and many others. And we stand on their shoulders. You know, it means that we have to acknowledge that the times are difficult, but the times were difficult before, as well, and people didn’t give up to fight. And that’s what makes me so sad, that many people, you know, are not willing and able to fight. I can understand that as a personal decision, and I’m not criticizing any individual, but that’s not a collective answer. The collective answer must be to challenge injustice. And when I say the law of — the power of the law, it does not mean that law is the solution, the only solution. No, law is one tool. Mobilizing international law meant in the last decades democraticizing international law. It was the domain of diplomats, of states, of corporations. And now we came into the play, and that’s an important step forwards. And that’s why we can continue on in this regard. ANJALI KAMAT : Wolfgang, you were quite involved in some of the struggles for accountability and justice in Syria. Can you give us an update on what’s happening with that? WOLFGANG KALECK : Yeah, that was a very striking example, what justice can achieve and what not. I mean, we have a 1-million-people diaspora community of Syrians in Germany. And with this community, we worked out, you know, a strategy of bringing cases in Germany and elsewhere in Europe against the Assad regime in the last 10 years, and it resulted in a number of judgments. The most important, in the beginning of 2022, the high court of the provincial town in Koblenz convicted a torturer, a torturer colonel. And the wonderful thing was that we, as European Center for Constitutional Rights, the lawyers, as well as our clients, were very clear that this is not justice. You know, this is not justice in the sense of comprehensive justice. This was not the end of impunity. But it was an important step forward. And because we had the privilege to work with the diaspora community, this was communicated back to Syria. So, you saw the pictures after the overthrow of the Assad regime, you know, the opening of the infamous torture prison, Sednaya. The accountability question, the question of truth and justice, was on the table from the very beginning, and you didn’t see that 20, 30 years ago in other parts of the world. That’s something new, and that’s an achievement. Of course, there are always setbacks. So, we cannot — we cannot support trials like in Syria, in Damascus, last month, where members of the Assad regime and others were, in a very short and quick trial, convicted to the death sentence. That is U.S. style. I mean, that’s the way how the U.S. set on trial on Saddam Hussein, the former dictator of Iraq. And that’s not in accordance with human rights standards. The accused, even the torturer, accused of torture and war crimes, they have the rights to a fair trial. And, of course, the death sentence is not in accordance with international human rights standards, despite the practices in China or in this country. AMY GOODMAN : You say, Wolfgang, you — last November, you hosted Syria’s National Commission for Transitional Justice here in Berlin, Germany. If you can explain what that is, and then tell us about the ceremony you witnessed in Paris last year honoring Syrian opposition figures associated with the photographer who smuggled out images of tortured bodies from Syria? It’s so interesting. Just before we talked to you, we talked to Mahmoud Khalil, who ultimately left Syria, he, himself, as a teenager, taking on the Assad regime. WOLFGANG KALECK : I mean, the Assad regime, father and son, ruled Syria over decades. And one of the — one of the most important tools they used was torture. So they installed a system of torture prisons. And so, in the moment when the democracy movement in the Arab Spring gained more and more support in Syria, the oppression went more and more brutal, including forced disappearances and including torturing and killing people. But there were — and that is also something we have to remind. You know, there were really courageous individuals, and one of them was the military photographer “Caesar,” who was supposed to photograph and document the dead corpses, dead of torture, and he, with the help of his group, smuggled these photographs out of Syria, and this allowed us, the worldwide human rights community, to go public and say, you know, “Here, we have a documentation of the crimes. There is no excuse. There is no legitimation.” And so, they laid, to a certain extent, the ground for the trials and also for the condemnation of the Assad regime. And they — in this ceremony you just mentioned of last year, they promised to continue, and that is also something. You know, they didn’t say, “OK, now the power in the Assad regime is overthrown, and now we’re facing a new era.” No, they know that this is another struggle. Another struggle began. And so, I understood also the position of the commission, which was installed by the new government. There are a lot of controversies. A friend of us, a colleague of us, was called to join the commission, and she left it earlier this year, because she says, “This is only one-sided. The new government doesn’t look into the crimes of all factions involved in the war in Syria of the last years, but only looks into the crimes of the Assad regime.” But this is what happens. This is the kind of struggles which are — you know, which are quite normal after the overthrow of a decadelong dictatorship. But it’s incredible, and this is the kind — also the kind of thing. You know, yesterday, I was speaking at Columbia University, and one student asked me, “Have you experienced surprises in your life?” Obviously, I have. And one of the surprises was, you know, five years ago, if you would have said that in Syria the Assad regime is overthrown, we wouldn’t have thought about it, and that there is a talk of accountability, that there is a commission, that there is a — they opened the prison. They search for truth. And that is also history. History is open in all directions. And that is something people have to realize again. And the question is: Do you want to throw yourself into these struggles, or do you want to be a bystander? ANJALI KAMAT : Wolfgang Kaleck, thank you so much, German human rights lawyer and founder of the European Center for Constitutional and Human Rights. His new book is titled The Power of Law: Reconciling Legality and International Justice . I’m Anjali Kamat in New York, with Amy Goodman in Berlin. To see Part 1 of our discussion with Wolfgang Kaleck, please go to democracynow.org.

articles.title: NATO chief says ‘no imminent danger’ but rearmament of Europe continues in full swing
articles.author: Ana Vračar
articles.content: More rearmament talks are underway in Brussels as European politicians continue building an increasingly tense anti-Russian discourse. On Wednesday, September 30, defense ministers and industry representatives joined the Euronews Defense and Space Summit , focusing on the bloc’s growing defense expenditure and member cooperation. The summit took place after weeks of allegations of hybrid attacks on EU members, which pushed the already tense rearmament narrative permeating the European political establishment up a couple more notches . It also followed, by only a couple of days, the Council of the EU’s announcement of the next phase of five European Defense Projects of Common Interest (EDPCIs) – projects that “allow EU countries to work together on major defense initiatives that are too large or too complex for individual countries to develop on their own.” Read more: “Militarization of rules and minds” in Europe threatens workers and welfare While separate, the two events shared several points in common, starting with a focus on increasing coordination between EU countries to arm more efficiently – and spend the billions of euros planned for defense over the coming years. They also emphasized sections of the military sector to receive the most attention – including drones and military capacities in Eastern Europe. This geographical focus goes beyond EU members, expanding to – at least – Ukraine and Moldova. Most EDPCIs – like the Drone and Counter-Drone European Resolve (DECODER) and the Eastern Flank Watch – list Ukraine as a partner. Ukrainian arms entrepreneurs were also present at the summit in Brussels, including leading figures from Fire Point, one of the country’s most prominent arms companies. Very imminent investments into arms While NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte stated in his summit intervention that there is “no imminent danger” to the alliance members’ territories, he and others did not hold back in offering anticipations of an unstable period. Belgian Minister of Defense Theo Francken, for one, anticipated “more hybrid threat actions” and an overall “dark winter for Europe” – a scenario he seems to want to address by spending more on arms and cutting social services, as he has explicitly stated on numerous occasions. “Europe has been very good in investing in soft power, in social security,” Francken said. “And it’s beautiful to have a pension system, to have social welfare systems when someone gets sick, when somebody loses his job – we have everything. But when there’s a war or there’s hybrid threats, we don’t have anything.” Considering the significant amount of money European countries have already invested into armament, his assessment that “we don’t have anything” is inaccurate at best. It also remains contested on a regular basis on the streets of many European cities, where trade unions, students, and peace movements continue to protest against austerity budgets that aim to provide for war. Europe needs a policy that builds security with its neighbors In addition to large-scale demonstrations against social security and labor cuts in France’s proposed 2027 budget and student strikes against conscription in Germany last week, mobilizations are expected to grow over the coming months – including an international youth strike in November. “We reject the militarization of our societies and support the young people who are refusing it,” the Stop ReArm Europe coalition wrote on September 23. “Thousands of high school students and university students across Europe are rising up to refuse militarization and the return of conscription.” Read more: German students say ‘we don’t want to go to war’ “Nearly 20 million children in the EU – one in four – live at risk of poverty or social exclusion,” the group added. “Meanwhile, governments have committed to military spending that the EU’s own Defense Commissioner, Andrius Kubilius, puts at €7 trillion by 2035.” “The trillions earmarked for militarized security will leave us staring down the barrel of a gun and indebted to global financiers,” Stop ReArm wrote, calling for a solidarity- and care-based alternative. “This must go hand in hand with a non-aligned foreign policy that resolves conflicts through diplomacy, upholds international law and human rights, and builds common security for all: security with our neighbors, not against them.”
